summary: Well-structured error hierarchy with correct prototype-chain restoration throughout. One self-contradictory deprecation notice and one semantic inaccuracy in the DuplicateIndexLabelError message are the only substantive issues; everything else is minor documentation or forward-compat polish.

findings.title: RepeatedDummyLabelError deprecation notice says removal is in v0.3.0, but the alias still exists in v0.3.0
findings.description: The JSDoc on `RepeatedDummyLabelError` reads: 'The old name will be removed in v0.3.0.' This file IS v0.3.0, so the alias should already be gone — or the comment is wrong. Downstream consumers who read the deprecation warning and removed their usage before upgrading to v0.3.0 are fine, but consumers who deferred removal expecting a v0.3.0 break will be silently surprised that the alias still compiles. More critically, if v0.3.5/v0.4.0 tooling scans for 'remove in vX.Y.Z' markers to automate cleanup, this stale marker will be missed or misfire.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) delete the alias entirely (it was promised gone in v0.3.0) and add a BREAKING CHANGE entry to CHANGELOG, or (b) update the comment to 'will be removed in v0.4.0' if the decision was made to extend the deprecation window. Do not leave a 'remove in v0.3.0' notice in a v0.3.0 file.

findings.title: DuplicateIndexLabelError message incorrectly states the allowed rule as 'at most twice (once upper, once lower)'
findings.description: The error message says 'A label may appear at most twice (once upper, once lower) within a single tensor-symbol's indices list.' But the class comment above it says this error fires on DECLARATION-TIME duplicates within a *single tensor-symbol's* indices list — i.e., the same label appearing more than once on one tensor. A single tensor symbol T^μ_μ is invalid regardless of variance; the 'once upper, once lower' rule applies to the *product* level (handled by IndexLabelCollisionError / VarianceMismatchError). The message therefore describes the wrong rule, which will confuse users trying to understand why T^μ_μ (a trace, which is valid in a product) is being rejected at declaration time.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the message to: `'Tensor \'${tensorName}\' has repeated index label \'${label}\' in its own index list. Each label must be unique within a single tensor symbol\'s declaration. To contract over a label, form a tensor-product and let Einstein summation apply.'`

findings.title: VarianceMismatchError message hard-codes v0.2.0 limitation but the error class ships in v0.3.0 which adds raise/lower
findings.description: The message body says 'v0.2.0 has no metric tensor available to raise/lower indices, so such a contraction is rejected'. v0.3.0 explicitly adds metric-tensor nodes and raise/lower helpers. The message is now factually wrong: v0.3.0 *does* have a metric, so the error should no longer cite a version-specific limitation but instead simply direct the user to the raise/lower API. This will also confuse v0.3.5/v0.4.0 users who encounter the error after the metric layer is fully operational.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the 'v0.2.0 has no metric tensor' clause. New message: `'Index label \'${label}\' appears twice but both with variance \'${variance}\'. Einstein contraction requires one upper and one lower occurrence. Use raise(operand, gInverse, \'${label}\') or lower(operand, g, \'${label}\') to adjust variance before contracting.'`

findings.title: FreeIndexMismatchError accepts a raw string message with no structured fields
findings.description: Every other error class in this file exposes structured public readonly fields (label, tensorName, variance, etc.) so callers can programmatically inspect the error without parsing the message string. FreeIndexMismatchError takes only a free-form string, making it impossible for downstream consumers (mathjs backend, v0.3.5) to extract the differing index signatures without fragile string parsing. This is inconsistent with the rest of the hierarchy and will be a pain point when v0.3.5 needs to surface structured diagnostics.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `public readonly expected: ReadonlyMap<string, 'upper'|'lower'> and public readonly actual: ReadonlyMap<string, 'upper'|'lower'>` fields (mirroring DimensionMismatchError's pattern), generate the message from them, and update all call sites.

findings.title: TensorInScalarOpError.op is untyped string; v0.4.0 op enum will diverge silently
findings.description: The `op` field is typed as `string`. When v0.4.0 introduces a typed `OpKind` union or enum for AST node operators, callers constructing TensorInScalarOpError will pass an `OpKind` value but the field will remain `string`, losing type safety at the throw site and making exhaustiveness checks impossible.
findings.suggested_fix: Define a local `ScalarOp = '*' | '/' | '^'` type (or import the AST op union when it exists) and type the field as `public readonly op: ScalarOp`. This is a non-breaking narrowing for current callers.

findings.title: InvalidKroneckerRankError message conflates 'rank' with 'index variance requirement'
findings.description: The message says 'must be rank-2 (exactly one upper + one lower index)'. The parenthetical describes a variance constraint, not a rank constraint — rank-2 means exactly two indices regardless of variance. The variance constraint is separately enforced by KroneckerVarianceError. Mixing the two in one message will confuse users who have rank-2 but same-variance indices: they will see the rank error message mentioning variance, then also see the variance error, and wonder which rule they violated.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the parenthetical to '(exactly two indices)' and remove the variance hint from this message. The variance hint belongs solely in KroneckerVarianceError.

findings.title: No evidence of instanceof-chain tests for the three new v0.3.0 error classes
findings.location: src/dimensional/errors.ts (all v0.3.0 additions: InvalidMetricRankError, MetricSignatureError, InvalidKroneckerRankError, KroneckerVarianceError, PartialDerivativeIndexVarianceError)
findings.description: The prototype-chain restoration pattern (`Object.setPrototypeOf`) is applied consistently, but its correctness can only be verified by an `instanceof UPTError` test after transpilation to ES5/CommonJS. The v0.2.0 errors presumably have such tests; the five new v0.3.0 error classes need equivalent coverage. Without it, a transpiler config change could silently break the `instanceof` discriminator that the module doc promises downstream consumers.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test block (e.g., in `tests/dimensional/errors.test.ts`) that constructs each new error class and asserts: `err instanceof UPTError === true`, `err instanceof <ConcreteClass> === true`, and `err.name === '<ConcreteClass>'`. Run under both ESM and CJS output targets.

strengths: Object.setPrototypeOf is applied in every constructor without exception, correctly restoring the prototype chain for ES5-transpiled targets — a common omission in custom Error subclasses.

Every v0.3.0 error class exposes structured public readonly fields (tensorName, label, actualRank, etc.) rather than encoding all information in the message string, enabling programmatic inspection by downstream consumers.
Error messages consistently cite the governing spec section (e.g., 'Per Part-VIII §VIII.2'), making it straightforward to cross-reference the spec when debugging.
The rename from RepeatedDummyLabelError to DuplicateIndexLabelError is well-motivated and the JSDoc explanation of why 'dummy' was a misnomer is clear and correct in its tensor-calculus reasoning.

The separation of IndexLabelCollisionError (>2 occurrences) from VarianceMismatchError (2 occurrences, wrong variance) is a clean, orthogonal decomposition that will make validator error-handling straightforward.

summary: Solid structural foundation for the v0.3.0 metric-layer validators; the module-cycle-avoidance pattern is well-executed. However, there are several correctness gaps: the Kronecker-delta validator silently accepts duplicate index labels, the partial-derivative validator discards `wrt`'s free indices without checking for collisions with `of`'s free indices, and the metric-tensor signature length is never validated against the actual tensor rank/dimension, making the signature check cosmetically correct but semantically vacuous.

findings.title: KroneckerDelta validator does not reject duplicate index labels (e.g., δ^μ_μ)
findings.description: validateMetricTensor explicitly checks `a.label === b.label` and throws MetricSignatureError. validateKroneckerDelta performs no such check. A node with indices [{label:'μ', variance:'upper'}, {label:'μ', variance:'lower'}] passes validation and is returned as having two free indices with label 'μ' — but δ^μ_μ is a contraction (trace = n), not a free-index expression. The freeIndices Map will silently overwrite the first entry with the second, producing a single lower-variance entry instead of flagging the contraction. This will cause downstream Einstein-contraction logic in v0.4.0 to miscount free indices.

findings.title: validatePartialDerivative discards wrt.freeIndices without checking collision with of.freeIndices
findings.description: The comment says 'discard wrt's own free indices' and the code does so, but it never checks whether any label in `wrtResult.freeIndices` collides with a label in `ofResult.freeIndices`. If `wrt` is itself a tensor expression with free indices that overlap `of`'s free indices, the silent discard hides an index-label collision that would produce an ill-formed output tensor. The existing collision check only guards `node.wrtIndex.label` against `ofResult.freeIndices`, which is correct but insufficient.

findings.title: isValidSignature does not validate that signature length matches tensor dimensionality
findings.description: isValidSignature only checks that each comma-separated token is '+' or '-'. It never verifies that the number of tokens equals the space dimension implied by the metric (e.g., 4 for spacetime, 3 for Euclidean). A signature '+,-' on a 4D metric passes validation silently. While the dimension count may not be available at this AST layer, the spec (§VIII.2) presumably ties signature length to the manifold dimension. At minimum, the validator should expose the parsed signature length in the result so callers can cross-check.
findings.suggested_fix: Expose `signatureRank: number` in `MetricTensorValidationResult` and compute it from the parsed parts. Callers that know the manifold dimension can then assert equality.

findings.title: validatePartialDerivative always assigns role 'field', even when of.role is 'connection' or future roles
findings.description: The comment cites 'Design §13 Q1 locked decision: default to field'. The code is `const role: Role = ofResult.role ?? 'field'`. However, if `ofResult.role` is defined (e.g., 'connection'), the partial derivative of a connection coefficient is a Riemann-tensor component — its role should arguably be 'curvature', not 'connection'. Blindly passing through `of.role` for all non-null roles will produce incorrect role annotations for v0.4.0 Christoffel/Riemann nodes. The locked decision may be intentionally deferring this, but the current code has no guard or TODO for the 'connection' case, making it a silent forward-compat hazard.

findings.title: MetricTensorValidationResult does not carry parsed signature; v0.4.0 Christoffel validators will need it
findings.description: Christoffel symbols (v0.4.0) require the metric signature to compute sign conventions for index raising/lowering. The current result type discards the parsed signature after validation. Downstream validators will have to re-parse `node.signature` from the original AST node, breaking the 'validate once, carry forward' invariant established by the InferContext accumulator pattern.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `readonly signatureParts: ReadonlyArray<'+' | '-'>` to `MetricTensorValidationResult` and populate it from the parsed parts in `validateMetricTensor`. This is additive and non-breaking.

findings.title: CovariantIndex.variance is hardcoded to literal 'lower' but TensorIndex.variance uses the Variance union type
findings.description: `CovariantIndex` declares `variance: 'lower'` as a string literal rather than `Variance` (which is imported from tensor.ts). This means a `TensorIndex` with `variance: 'lower'` cannot be assigned to `CovariantIndex` without a cast if `Variance` is a union type that includes 'lower'. It also means the PartialDerivativeIndexVarianceError check (`node.wrtIndex.variance !== 'lower'`) is a type-level tautology — TypeScript already knows it's 'lower'. The check is unreachable at compile time if the node is properly typed, but the runtime guard is still needed for untyped inputs.

findings.title: No test exercises the δ^μ_μ duplicate-label path (which is currently a silent bug, not a thrown error)
findings.description: Because the duplicate-label check is missing (see bug finding above), there is no test asserting that δ^μ_μ throws. Once the bug is fixed, a test must be added. Even before the fix, a test asserting the *current* (broken) behavior would make the regression visible.

findings.title: No test verifies that wrt.freeIndices colliding with of.freeIndices is caught
findings.description: The collision check for `node.wrtIndex.label` vs `ofResult.freeIndices` is tested (presumably), but the case where `wrtResult.freeIndices` itself overlaps `ofResult.freeIndices` is not guarded in code and therefore cannot be tested. Once the bug fix is applied, a test for this path is required.

findings.title: JSDoc for validatePartialDerivative does not document that wrt.freeIndices are silently discarded
findings.description: The JSDoc lists two thrown errors but does not mention that `wrtResult.freeIndices` is intentionally discarded. This is a non-obvious semantic choice (∂_μ T^ν is free in ν and μ, not in whatever indices `wrt` itself carries). Future maintainers may mistake the discard for a bug.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add to the JSDoc:
```
 * Note: `wrt`'s own free indices are intentionally discarded; the only
 * index contributed by the differentiation operator is `wrtIndex` (lower).
 * Per §VIII.4 the `wrt` operand's role is purely dimensional — its free
 * indices do not propagate to the output.
```

strengths: Module-cycle-avoidance via injected `validateChild` callback is correctly implemented and matches the established `computeContraction` pattern — this will compose cleanly with v0.4.0 covariant-derivative nodes.
The `unknown` typing on `TensorPartialDerivativeNode.of` / `.wrt` with an explicit comment explaining the cycle-avoidance rationale is clear and intentional, not sloppy.
validateMetricTensor's mixed-variance check correctly identifies that g_μν and g^μν are distinct objects and directs users to raise()/lower() helpers — good API-ergonomics guardrail.
The TODO comment for InverseMetricInconsistencyWarning is well-scoped, references the locked design decision, and correctly defers to v0.3.5 without leaving an open-ended placeholder.
freeIndices Map construction is consistent across all three validators, making the shape predictable for the InferContext accumulator merge in validator.ts.
Role passthrough defaulting to 'field' is explicitly tied to a locked design decision reference, making it auditable.

summary: Constructors are clean and the alpha-conversion logic in raise()/lower() is mostly correct, but there are two concrete bugs: the fresh-label collision set omits the metric's own index labels (allowing silent dummy-index collisions), and the alpha-conversion always renames index[1] even when index[0] already carries the target label — producing a wrong contraction when the caller's label happens to match gInverse.indices[1].label. Several forward-compat and API-ergonomics issues also warrant attention.

findings.title: `taken` set in raise()/lower() does not include the metric's own free-index labels, allowing dummy-index collision
findings.description: After alpha-conversion, `renamedGInverse` introduces a new free index `renamed`. The `taken` set is seeded only from `operandLabels` plus `label`. If `gInverse.indices[1].label` (the base for `freshLabel`) happens to already be a free index in `operand` under a *different* name, that is handled — but if the metric itself has a second index whose label collides with another free index in the operand that was not yet in `taken` because it was added after the set was built, the collision is missed. More concretely: `taken` never includes `gInverse.indices[0].label`. If `gInverse.indices[0].label` equals some other free-index label in `operand` (not `label`), `freshLabel` may return a string that equals `gInverse.indices[0].label`, which is already used as the contraction dummy — producing two distinct free indices with the same label in the resulting tensor-product, violating the Einstein-summation uniqueness invariant. The fix is to also add all of the metric's own index labels to `taken` before calling `freshLabel`.

findings.title: Alpha-conversion always renames index[1] regardless of which metric index matches `label`, producing wrong contraction when `label === gInverse.indices[1].label`
findings.description: The code unconditionally maps `gInverse.indices[0] → label` (the contraction dummy) and `gInverse.indices[1] → renamed` (the new free index). If the caller passes a `label` that already equals `gInverse.indices[1].label` (not index[0]), the contraction dummy is still placed at index[0] and the new free index at index[1] — but the resulting `renamedGInverse` has index[1].label = `renamed` (a fresh label), so the contraction with `operand` on `label` is correct only by accident when `label !== gInverse.indices[1].label`. When `label === gInverse.indices[1].label`, the rename of index[1] to `renamed` discards the intended contraction slot and the contraction on `label` is still driven by index[0] — which is fine — but the *fresh* label is derived from `gInverse.indices[1].label` which equals `label`, so `freshLabel(label, taken)` where `taken` already contains `label` will produce `label_1`, which is correct. The deeper issue is that the code does not handle the symmetric case where the caller intends index[1] to be the contraction dummy (e.g., the metric is written g^{νμ} and the caller wants to contract on ν). The API silently ignores which slot the user intended and always uses slot 0 as the dummy, which is only correct because the metric is symmetric — but this assumption is not documented or asserted.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit assertion or doc comment: `// Metric symmetry assumed: g^{ab} = g^{ba}; index[0] is always chosen as the contraction dummy.` If asymmetric metrics are ever supported (v0.4.0 torsion), this must be revisited. For now, add: `// INVARIANT: caller must not rely on which slot is the dummy.`

findings.title: `collectFreeIndexLabels` silently drops indices that appear on both upper and lower sides (net-zero contracted indices)
findings.description: `validate(node).freeIndices` returns counts per label. The loop only records a label if `counts.upper > 0` OR `counts.lower > 0`, but if a label appears once upper and once lower (a contracted pair, counts.upper === 1, counts.lower === 1), it is still iterated — and the `if (counts.upper > 0)` branch fires first, recording it as 'upper'. This means a dummy (contracted) index is incorrectly treated as a free upper index. Consequently, `raise()` will throw `RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError` with the misleading message that the label is 'already upper', when in fact it is a contracted dummy that should not be raiseable at all. The fix is to skip labels where both counts are non-zero.

findings.title: `raise()`/`lower()` return a bare `TensorProductNode` with no dimension propagation, breaking v0.3.5 numerical backend
findings.description: `TensorProductNode` presumably carries a `dim` field (or the validator infers it). The returned node `{ kind: 'tensor-product', args: [renamedGInverse, operand] }` omits any `dim` field. When v0.3.5 attaches a mathjs numerical backend that reads `node.dim` directly (rather than re-running the validator), it will see `undefined` and either crash or silently treat the result as dimensionless. The dimension of the raised/lowered tensor should be `operand.dim` (the metric is dimensionless in natural units, or its dimension should be composed). At minimum, a `dim` field should be threaded through.
findings.suggested_fix: return { kind: 'tensor-product', args: [renamedGInverse, operand], dim: operand.dim };

findings.title: `RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError` is private but `MetricSignatureError` is public — inconsistent error surface makes catch-blocks fragile for callers
findings.description: Callers of `raise()`/`lower()` need to distinguish 'wrong metric variance' (MetricSignatureError, public) from 'wrong label' (RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError, private/unexported). Because `RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError` is not exported, callers cannot write `catch (e) { if (e instanceof RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError) ... }` — they must fall back to string-matching `e.message` or catching the base `UPTError`. Design §6 says this is intentional, but the spec should be updated to clarify what callers are expected to catch, or the error should be exported.
findings.suggested_fix: Either export `RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError` (preferred for testability) or document explicitly in the JSDoc of `raise()`/`lower()` that the label-error is a subclass of `UPTError` and callers should catch `UPTError` and inspect `e.name === 'RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError'`.

findings.title: `pderiv` does not validate that `wrt` is a coordinate expression, which will cause silent AST invalidity for v0.4.0 Christoffel symbols
findings.description: The Christoffel symbol constructor (v0.4.0) will need `pderiv` nodes whose `wrt` field is a coordinate tensor. Currently `pderiv` accepts any `ExprNode` for `wrt` with no structural check. When the Christoffel builder pattern-matches on `pderiv.wrt.kind`, it will need to handle arbitrary expression kinds. Adding a narrower type or a runtime assertion now (e.g., `wrt.kind === 'tensor'`) would make the v0.4.0 constraint explicit and catch misuse early.

findings.title: `freshLabel` base is always `gInverse.indices[1].label` — if that label is the empty string, the scheme produces `_1`, `_2`, … which are valid but semantically opaque
findings.description: If a metric node is constructed with `indices[1].label === ''` (possible via the `metric()` constructor which has no validation), `freshLabel('', taken)` produces `_1`. This is not caught anywhere and will propagate into the AST as an index label `_1`, which may collide with user-chosen labels of the same form. The `metric()` constructor should validate that index labels are non-empty strings.

findings.title: No tests for the alpha-conversion collision case: `gInverse.indices[1].label` already present in operand free indices
findings.description: The entire purpose of `freshLabel` is to avoid collisions. There should be a test where `operand` has a free index whose label equals `gInverse.indices[1].label`, verifying that the resulting `TensorProductNode` does not contain two free indices with the same label. Without this test, the collision-avoidance logic is untested and the bug in finding #1 above would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: No test verifying that `raise()` throws `MetricSignatureError` (not `RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError`) when given a covariant metric
findings.description: The guard `gInverse.indices[0].variance !== 'upper'` is the first check in `raise()`. A test passing a covariant metric (both-lower) to `raise()` should assert that the thrown error is specifically a `MetricSignatureError`. Without this, a refactor that swaps the check order could silently change which error is thrown.
findings.suggested_fix: expect(() => raise(operand, covariantMetric, 'μ')).toThrow(MetricSignatureError);

findings.title: JSDoc for `raise()` says 'one of gInverse's labels is renamed to match label' but does not specify *which* index (0 or 1) becomes the dummy
findings.description: The implementation always uses index[0] as the contraction dummy and index[1] as the new free index. The JSDoc says 'one of gInverse's labels' without specifying which. This ambiguity will confuse maintainers implementing v0.4.0 Christoffel symbols who need to know the exact slot assignment.
findings.suggested_fix: Update JSDoc: 'index[0] of gInverse is renamed to `label` (the Einstein-summation dummy); index[1] is renamed to a fresh label (the resulting free index). Metric symmetry is assumed.'

strengths: The `freshLabel` function is deterministic and its contract (Part-VIII §VIII.5 TENSOR-RULE) is correctly cited in the JSDoc.
`RaiseLowerInvalidLabelError` correctly calls `Object.setPrototypeOf` to fix the TypeScript `instanceof` prototype chain issue — a subtle correctness detail that is easy to miss.
The `kronecker()` constructor correctly defaults `dim` to `DIMENSIONLESS` and documents the Design §13 Q3 lock, making the intent clear for future maintainers.
Variance guards in `raise()`/`lower()` are symmetric and throw typed errors (`MetricSignatureError`) rather than generic `Error`, which is consistent with the library's error surface design.
The `collectFreeIndexLabels` helper correctly delegates to `validate()` rather than re-implementing free-index collection, keeping the logic DRY and consistent with the validator's invariants.

summary: The validator is well-structured and handles the v0.3.0 metric-layer additions (metric-tensor, kronecker-delta, tensor-partial-derivative) consistently with the existing tensor-symbol/tensor-product pattern. Several correctness issues exist: a shared-mutable-state bug in the integral/derivative cases, a silent free-index leak in the '+'/'-' path when the first operand has an empty freeIndices map, a missing free-index check in validateEquation, and a throw-vs-record inconsistency for TensorInScalarOpError that breaks the violations contract.

findings.title: integral/derivative cases share ctx.freeIndices with child infer() calls, leaking tensor free-indices into the parent accumulator
findings.description: Both `integral` and `derivative` spread `ctx` into child calls: `{ ...ctx, path: ... }`. The spread is shallow, so `freeIndices` is the *same Map reference* in the child context. If `node.integrand` or `node.of` is a tensor-symbol (or any tensor node), its free-indices are written directly into the parent's `ctx.freeIndices` accumulator. This is incorrect: the integration/differentiation variable and integrand are not free indices of the result in the same sense as a bare tensor-symbol. The correct pattern (used by `op '+'` and `op '*'`) is `inferArgLocal`, which creates a fresh local Map. For `integral`, the result should have no free indices (or the integrand's free indices minus the integration variable's, which is a more complex rule); at minimum the current code is wrong because it unconditionally promotes child tensor free-indices to the parent.

findings.title: TensorInScalarOpError is thrown (not recorded as a violation), breaking the ValidationResult contract for '*', '/', '^' with tensor operands
findings.description: `validate()` and `validateEquation()` are documented to return a `ValidationResult` with `ok: false` and a populated `violations` array on any dimensional or structural error. However, when a tensor-valued operand appears inside `op '*'`, `op '/'`, or `op '^'`, the code throws `TensorInScalarOpError` instead of pushing a violation and returning `null`. This means callers that do `const r = validate(expr)` and check `r.ok` will never see the error — they get an uncaught exception instead. The `FreeIndexMismatchError` in the `'+'`/`'-'` path has the same issue. Both error types should be caught inside `infer()` and converted to violations, or the public API contract must be explicitly documented as 'may throw'.

findings.title: op '+'/'-' propagates firstFI even when it is an empty map, silently suppressing free-index information from later operands
findings.description: After the loop, the code merges `firstFI` into `ctx.freeIndices`. If `args[0]` is a scalar (empty freeIndices) and `args[1]` is also scalar, this is fine. But if `args[0]` is a scalar and `args[1]` is a tensor, the `freeIndicesEqual` check correctly throws `FreeIndexMismatchError`. However, if both are scalars, `firstFI` is empty and nothing is merged — also fine. The subtle bug: if `args[0]` is a tensor with free indices and `args[1]` is also a tensor with the *same* free indices (the valid case), `firstFI` holds the correct map and is merged — correct. BUT: the merge uses `ctx.freeIndices.set(label, counts)` which *overwrites* any pre-existing entry from a sibling subtree that was already merged into `ctx.freeIndices` by a prior sibling at the same level. This is only safe because `op '+'` is the only place that merges, and it does so once at the end. However, if the same label appears in `ctx.freeIndices` from a *parent* context (because `ctx` is shared by reference in the integral/derivative spread-ctx bug above), the overwrite is incorrect. This is a secondary consequence of finding #1 but is independently observable.

findings.title: validateEquation does not check free-index agreement between LHS and RHS
findings.description: `validateEquation` checks dimensional homogeneity (`equals(lhsDim, rhsDim)`) but does not check that `lhsCtx.freeIndices` and `rhsCtx.freeIndices` are equal. A tensor equation like `T^μν = S^μ` (rank-2 LHS, rank-1 RHS) would pass the validator with `ok: true` if both sides happen to have the same dimension, because the free-index mismatch is never tested. The comment 'Equation-level free-index agreement checks are deferred to Task 7' acknowledges this, but the omission is a correctness gap that will silently pass invalid equations through the v0.3.0 release and into the v0.3.5 numerical backend.

findings.title: resolveChildForPartialDerivative accesses typed.role without a type guard, will be undefined for non-tensor-symbol nodes
findings.description: `typed.role` is accessed on the result of `validateTensorSymbol(typed)` — but `role` is a property of `TensorSymbolNode`, not of `ChildValidationResult`. The code reads `typed.role` (the raw node's role) and attaches it to the returned `PartialDerivativeChildResult`. This is fine for the `tensor-symbol` branch. However, the cast `const typed = node as ExprNode` at the top of the function means that if a caller passes a non-TensorSymbolNode into this branch (impossible today but possible if the dispatch logic in `validatePartialDerivative` changes), `typed.role` would be `undefined` without a TypeScript error because `ExprNode` does not declare `role`. More concretely: the `role` field is read from the *node* not from the *validateTensorSymbol result*, so if `validateTensorSymbol` normalises or rejects the role, the returned role bypasses that normalisation.

findings.title: op '^' base-probe violations are not forwarded when baseDim is null
findings.description: `inferArgLocal` for the base node forwards violations to `ctx.violations` (because `localCtx.violations` is the same reference as `ctx.violations`). So violations ARE forwarded. However, when `baseDim === null`, the function returns `null` immediately *before* checking the exponent. This means a malformed exponent (e.g. a non-symbol) is silently ignored when the base also fails. This is a minor UX issue: the user sees only the base error, not both errors simultaneously. More importantly, the early return on `baseDim === null` skips the `baseProbe.freeIndices.size > 0` tensor-rejection check — so a tensor base that also fails dimension inference will not throw `TensorInScalarOpError`. The tensor-rejection check should come before the null-return.

findings.title: tensor-partial-derivative case in infer() does not guard against violations thrown by validatePartialDerivative, unlike tensor-product which has an explicit try/catch comment
findings.description: The `tensor-product` case wraps `computeContraction` in a try/catch with a comment explaining that errors from the contraction are part of the public surface. The `tensor-partial-derivative` case calls `validatePartialDerivative` with no try/catch. If `validatePartialDerivative` throws (e.g. a `VarianceMismatchError` on the derivative index), the exception propagates uncaught through `infer()` and out of `validate()`, breaking the violations-based contract. For v0.4.0 (Christoffel symbols, covariant derivative), this case will be exercised heavily and the inconsistency will cause test failures.

findings.title: validate() and validateEquation() silently swallow thrown TensorInScalarOpError / FreeIndexMismatchError — callers have no way to distinguish 'violations array' errors from 'thrown' errors without wrapping every call in try/catch
findings.description: The public API surface (`validate`, `validateEquation`) returns `ValidationResult` for dimensional errors but throws for structural tensor errors. This dual-mode error reporting forces every consumer to both check `result.ok` AND wrap in try/catch. Bridge modules (9+ consumers per the DimensionValidationReport comment) will each need to replicate this boilerplate. For v0.3.5 (mathjs backend) this is especially problematic because the numerical backend will call `validate()` in a hot path.

findings.title: No test coverage for the integral/derivative + tensor-symbol combination that triggers the shared-freeIndices bug (finding #1)
findings.description: The shared-ctx spread bug in `integral` and `derivative` is only observable when the integrand or differentiated expression is a tensor-symbol (or any tensor node). A test like `validate({ kind: 'integral', integrand: { kind: 'tensor-symbol', ... }, over: { kind: 'symbol', ... } })` would expose the bug by showing free-indices in the result that should not be there. Without such a test, the bug will survive into v0.3.5.

findings.title: No test verifies that validate() returns ok:false (not throws) for tensor operands inside op '*'/'/'
findings.description: Given finding #2 (TensorInScalarOpError is thrown, not recorded), any existing test that calls `validate()` with a tensor inside `op '*'` and asserts `result.ok === false` would already be failing. If no such test exists, the bug is undetected. The test suite should include a case that exercises this path and asserts the expected behavior (whether that is 'throws' or 'ok:false with violation').

findings.title: try/catch in tensor-product case is a no-op pass-through and adds noise
findings.description: The try/catch block around `computeContraction` catches `err` and immediately re-throws it with `throw err`. The comment says 'propagate them so callers / tests can catch by type' — but this is what happens without the try/catch. The block adds 4 lines of noise and may mislead future maintainers into thinking some transformation is happening.

findings.title: resolveChildForPartialDerivative parameter typed as `unknown` instead of `ExprNode`, hiding the type contract
findings.description: The function signature is `(node: unknown, parentCtx: InferContext)` with an immediate cast `const typed = node as ExprNode`. The `unknown` type was presumably chosen to match the callback signature expected by `validatePartialDerivative`. If `PartialDerivativeChildResult`'s resolver callback is typed as `(node: unknown) => ...`, that type should be tightened to `ExprNode` in `metric-validators.ts`. Using `unknown` here obscures the contract and disables TypeScript's narrowing assistance in the function body.

strengths: inferArgLocal is a well-designed primitive that correctly isolates child freeIndices maps from the parent accumulator — the op '*'/'/' and op '^' cases use it correctly.
The exhaustiveness guard in the default case (with the never-typed _exhaustive variable) is a robust forward-compat pattern that will catch unhandled ExprNode arms at compile time.
resolveChildForContraction correctly breaks the module cycle between validator.ts and tensor.ts by injecting the resolver as a callback, avoiding circular imports.
freeIndicesEqual and formatFreeIndices are clean, well-named utilities with clear single responsibilities.
The DimensionValidationReport interface is correctly extracted as a shared type for the 9+ bridge consumers, eliminating per-module redeclaration.
The scope notes at the top of the file are honest and specific (index-rank mismatch, special-function dimensionlessness), which is valuable for future maintainers and reviewers.
The freeIndices accumulator design (shared Map by reference, merged only at the outermost level for tensor-product) is architecturally sound for the non-integral/derivative cases.

summary: BE-37 is a well-documented reformulation of the invalid VSL ansatz into the canonical Shapiro delay. The scalar layer is clean; the v0.3.0 eikonal tensor layer introduces several correctness and forward-compat issues worth addressing before v0.3.5/v0.4.0 land.

findings.title: `pderiv` dimension is DIMENSIONLESS only if LENGTH/LENGTH cancels — but the cancellation is not guaranteed by the AST encoding
findings.description: The comment states `dim = LENGTH/LENGTH = DIMENSIONLESS` for `∂_μ S`. This is physically correct (S has dim LENGTH, x^α has dim LENGTH), but it relies on `pderiv()` internally computing `dim(S) / dim(wrt)`. If `pderiv` instead inherits `dim(S)` unchanged (a common implementation choice — the derivative carries the numerator dimension and the denominator dimension is tracked in the index metadata), then `dmu_S.dim = LENGTH`, not `DIMENSIONLESS`. The downstream `contract()` would then produce `DIMENSIONLESS * LENGTH * LENGTH = LENGTH²`, causing `validateBE37EikonalDimensions()` to return `ok: false` silently (or worse, `ok: true` with a wrong inferred dimension if the validator has a bug). The comment in the decision-record section acknowledges the `raise()` alpha-conversion subtlety but does not address this `pderiv` dimension convention. Without seeing `metric.ts`, the actual behavior is ambiguous, making this a latent critical bug if the convention differs from the assumption.
findings.suggested_fix: Explicitly assert the dimension at the call site: `const dmu_S = pderiv(S_eikonal, x_coord, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' });` should be followed by a compile-time or runtime assertion `assert(dmu_S.dim === DIMENSIONLESS, 'pderiv dim mismatch')`. Alternatively, if `pderiv` carries the numerator dim, declare `S_eikonal` with `DIMENSIONLESS` and document that the LENGTH/LENGTH cancellation is pre-applied. Add a unit test in `tests/dimensional/be-37-eikonal.test.ts` that checks `validate(dmu_S).inferredDimension === DIMENSIONLESS`.

findings.title: `contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S, dnu_S)` — three-argument `contract` signature not established in the public API
findings.description: The import is `import { tsym, contract } from '../../dimensional/tensor.js'`. The standard Einstein-contraction `contract(A, B)` pairs one repeated index between two tensors. The call `contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S, dnu_S)` passes THREE tensors. If `contract` is a binary function (the most common implementation), this silently drops `dnu_S` (TypeScript will not error if the third argument is ignored via rest params or overloads). Even if a ternary overload exists, the semantics — whether it means `(g⊗dmu_S⊗dnu_S)` fully contracted, or sequential binary contractions — is unspecified in the visible code. The decision-record comment says 'direct contraction — μ pairs … ν pairs … in one tensor-product', implying a single ternary call, but this is non-standard and may not be implemented.
findings.suggested_fix: Use sequential binary contractions to be safe and explicit: `const gS_mu = contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S); // contracts μ, leaves ν-upper free` then `const eikonal_scalar = contract(gS_mu, dnu_S); // contracts ν`. Export `BE37_EIKONAL_LHS = eikonal_scalar`. This is unambiguous regardless of whether a ternary overload exists. Add a test asserting `BE37_EIKONAL_LHS` has zero free indices (rank 0).

findings.title: `R_near_m === R_far_m` produces `ln(1) = 0` silently — evaluator should warn or reject
findings.description: The guard rejects `R_near_m > R_far_m` but allows `R_near_m === R_far_m`. In that case `Math.log(1) = 0` and the function returns exactly 0, which is physically meaningless (light path with zero impact parameter difference). This is not a NaN/Infinity, so it silently propagates. For the v0.3.5 mathjs backend this will produce a zero result that could mask integration errors.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `if (R_near_m >= R_far_m) { throw new RangeError(...) }` (strict inequality), or at minimum add a `if (R_near_m === R_far_m) console.warn(...)`. The guard message already says 'ratio inside ln must be ≥ 1' — change to '> 1' and use strict `>=` in the condition.

findings.title: `BE37_C_CUBED` uses a bare `^` op-node but the dimensional validator may not handle non-integer symbolic exponents
findings.description: `THREE_EXP` is a `sym('3', DIMENSIONLESS)` — a symbol node, not a numeric literal. If the dimensional validator's `^` handler requires the exponent to be a numeric literal (kind: 'number') to compute `dim(base)^n`, it will fail to infer the dimension of `BE37_C_CUBED` and propagate an unknown/error dimension into `BE37_PREFACTOR`. The result would be `validateBE37Dimensions()` returning `ok: false` with a misleading error. This is a latent bug that depends on the validator implementation.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `const THREE_EXP: ExprNode = sym('3', DIMENSIONLESS)` with `const THREE_EXP: ExprNode = { kind: 'number', value: 3, dim: DIMENSIONLESS }` (or whatever the numeric-literal node kind is in the AST schema). This makes the exponent unambiguously a literal integer for the validator's power-rule handler.

findings.title: PPN parameter γ is hardcoded to 1 with no extension point for v0.4.0 PPN framework
findings.description: The honest-claude scope note correctly flags that the encoded coefficient is `2GM/c³` (γ=1 GR-canonical), not the general PPN form `(1+γ)GM/c³`. v0.4.0 will introduce Christoffel symbols and covariant derivatives, and a PPN-parameterized Shapiro delay is a natural v0.4.0 target. Currently there is no `gamma` parameter in `ShapiroInputs`, no `BE37_GAMMA` symbol node, and no `BE37_PPN_PREFACTOR` AST variant. Adding γ later will be a breaking API change to both the evaluator signature and the exported AST nodes.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an optional `gamma?: number = 1` field to `ShapiroInputs` and use `(1 + gamma) * G_SI * M_kg` in the evaluator. Add a `BE37_GAMMA: ExprNode = sym('gamma', DIMENSIONLESS)` export and a `BE37_PPN_PREFACTOR` variant that uses it. Mark both as `@since v0.3.0` so v0.4.0 can promote them without a breaking change.

findings.title: Eikonal `x_coord` uses label `α` but `dmu_S`/`dnu_S` use labels `μ`/`ν` — index-label mismatch may confuse v0.4.0 covariant-derivative substitution
findings.description: `x_coord` is declared with index label `α` (upper), but `pderiv` is called with `{ label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }` and `{ label: 'ν', variance: 'lower' }`. The `wrt` argument's label (`α`) and the output index label (`μ`, `ν`) are different. If `pderiv` uses the `wrt` label as the output index label (a natural implementation), the resulting node has label `α`, not `μ`, and the subsequent `contract` with `g_inverse` (which has labels `μ`, `ν`) will find no matching pair and produce a rank-4 tensor instead of a scalar. If `pderiv` uses the third argument's label as the output label (overriding `wrt`), the `α` label on `x_coord` is vestigial and confusing. Either way, the label relationship is ambiguous and will be a maintenance hazard when v0.4.0 replaces `pderiv` with `∇_μ`.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) rename `x_coord` to use label `μ` and declare separate `x_coord_nu` with label `ν`, making the `wrt` label match the output index label, or (b) document explicitly in a comment which label `pderiv` uses for the output index and add a runtime assertion `assert(dmu_S.indices[0].label === 'μ')` immediately after the `pderiv` call.

findings.title: `validateBE37Dimensions` and `validateBE37EikonalDimensions` return raw `DimensionValidationReport` with no bridge-id tagging
findings.description: Both validation functions return a plain `DimensionValidationReport`. When the bridge registry calls all per-bridge validators in bulk (e.g., in a CI sweep), a failing report has no `bridgeId` or `equationLabel` field, making it impossible to identify which bridge failed without wrapping at the call site. Other bridges in the catalog likely have the same issue, but it is worth fixing here as a pattern-setter for v0.3.0.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the return type to `DimensionValidationReport & { bridgeId: 37; form: 'scalar' | 'eikonal' }` and add those fields: `return { ok: eq.ok, lhsDim: ..., rhsDim: ..., bridgeId: 37, form: 'scalar' }`. Alternatively, add a `label` string field to `DimensionValidationReport` in the validator types and populate it here.

findings.title: No test verifies that `BE37_EIKONAL_LHS` is rank-0 (scalar) — the contraction correctness is untested
findings.description: The most critical correctness property of the eikonal encoding is that `contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S, dnu_S)` produces a rank-0 node (all indices contracted). There is no test asserting `BE37_EIKONAL_LHS.indices.length === 0` or that `validateBE37EikonalDimensions().ok === true`. Given the three-argument `contract` ambiguity and the `pderiv` dimension convention uncertainty flagged above, this is the highest-value missing test.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `tests/bridges/be-37-eikonal.test.ts` with: (1) `expect(BE37_EIKONAL_LHS.indices?.length ?? 0).toBe(0)` — rank-0 check; (2) `expect(validateBE37EikonalDimensions().ok).toBe(true)` — dimension check; (3) `expect(validate(dmu_S).inferredDimension).toEqual(DIMENSIONLESS)` — pderiv dimension convention check.

findings.title: Numerical evaluator has no test for the canonical Sun-grazing benchmark (53 μs)
findings.description: The JSDoc states 'For the Sun (M_sun = 1.989e30 kg) with light passing from 1 AU to grazing R_sun, Δt_one-way ≈ 53 μs' but no test asserts this. The bracket-check in the comment is the only validation. If `G_SI` or `c_SI` constants are wrong, or if the formula has a sign/factor error, no automated test will catch it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the test file: `expect(evaluateShapiroDelay({ M_kg: 1.989e30, R_far_m: 1.496e11, R_near_m: 6.957e8 })).toBeCloseTo(53e-6, 1)` (tolerance ±5 μs, i.e., ~10%). Also test the `R_near_m >= R_far_m` guard throws.

findings.title: Decision-record comment on `raise()` alpha-conversion is in production source, not a design doc
findings.description: The multi-paragraph comment explaining why `raise()` was NOT used (alpha-conversion collision) is valuable design rationale but belongs in `docs/planning/v0.3.0-Bridge-Selection.md` or an ADR, not inline in production source. It makes the file significantly harder to read and will confuse v0.4.0 contributors who see a long explanation of a path not taken.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the `raise()` rationale to `docs/adr/be-37-eikonal-encoding.md`. Replace the inline block with a one-line comment: `// Direct contraction chosen over raise(); see docs/adr/be-37-eikonal-encoding.md for rationale.`

findings.title: `BE37_TWO` and `THREE_EXP` are unexported/exported inconsistently
findings.description: `BE37_TWO` is exported (useful for tests), but `THREE_EXP` is `const` (unexported). If a test wants to verify `BE37_C_CUBED`'s structure, it cannot access the exponent node. This is minor but inconsistent with the pattern of exporting all lemma nodes.
findings.suggested_fix: Either export `THREE_EXP` as `export const BE37_THREE_EXP` for consistency, or make `BE37_TWO` unexported too (since it is only used internally in `BE37_PREFACTOR`). Pick one pattern and apply it uniformly.

strengths: The reformulation rationale (VSL → Shapiro delay) is exceptionally well-documented with primary literature citations, the Ellis-Uzan critique, and honest scope notes about what the reformulation does and does not recover.
The dimensional analysis walkthrough in the JSDoc is complete and correct: G·M/c³ → [T] is verified step-by-step, and the log-argument dimensionlessness is explicitly called out.
The `evaluateShapiroDelay` input validation is thorough: finite-check, positivity-check, and ordering-check (R_near ≤ R_far) are all present with informative error messages.

The decision to use the direct three-tensor contraction rather than `raise()` is physically motivated and the alpha-conversion hazard is explicitly documented — showing awareness of the v0.3.0 tensor layer's subtleties.
The one-way vs. round-trip distinction (2GM/c³ vs. 4GM/c³) is clearly flagged in both the JSDoc and the bracket-check section, preventing a common factor-of-2 confusion.
The PPN γ=1 limitation is honestly disclosed in the scope notes, making it easy for a v0.4.0 contributor to know exactly what needs to be generalized.

The eikonal structural form is correctly identified as the tensor-structural origin of the scalar Shapiro delay, and the forward-compat anchor for v0.4.0 covariant derivative substitution is explicitly noted.

summary: A thorough, well-structured spec for the v0.3.0 metric layer. The invariants are largely implementable and internally consistent, but several rules contain subtle logical gaps, one outright contradiction, and a few forward-compat hazards that will cause pain in v0.3.5 and v0.4.0.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE: pderiv-dim-divides-by-wrt-dim contradicts TENSOR-RULE: pderiv-ignores-wrt-own-indices
findings.description: pderiv-dim-divides-by-wrt-dim states the output dim is `divide(of.dim, wrt.dim)`. pderiv-ignores-wrt-own-indices states '`wrt` is used for its dim only'. But the worked example in §VIII.8 passes the SAME `x_coord` tensor-symbol (dim LENGTH, rank-1) as `wrt` for BOTH `dmu_S` and `dnu_S`. If `wrt.dim` is the dim of the whole tensor-symbol node (LENGTH), the rule is consistent. However, the rule text says 'the coordinate `x^μ` has units [m]', implying the dim of a single coordinate component — not the tensor. For a rank-1 coordinate tensor, `wrt.dim` is unambiguous only if the spec explicitly states it means the node-level `dim` field (not a per-component or per-index dim). The spec never makes this explicit. An implementor could reasonably read 'wrt.dim' as the dim of the coordinate component being differentiated with respect to, which for a rank-1 tensor is the same as the node dim — but for a rank-2 `wrt` (e.g., differentiating with respect to a metric component) the two readings diverge. The spec must clarify that `wrt.dim` means the node-level `dim` field of the `wrt` ExprNode.
findings.suggested_fix: In pderiv-dim-divides-by-wrt-dim, replace 'wrt.dim' with 'the `dim` field of the `wrt` ExprNode (the node-level uniform-component dimension, per §VIII.10's uniform-component-dim assumption)'. Add a note: 'When `wrt` is a rank-N tensor with N > 0, this is the shared component dimension, not a per-index quantity.'

findings.title: MetricSignatureError reused for two unrelated validation failures
findings.description: `MetricSignatureError` is specified as the error for (a) mixed-variance metric indices (§VIII.2 rule metric-tensor-indices-same-variance), (b) malformed signature strings (§VIII.2 rule metric-tensor-signature-required), and (c) passing a lower-variance metric to `raise()` (§VIII.5 rule raise-requires-upper-variance-inverse-metric). These are three structurally distinct failure modes. Sharing one error class makes programmatic error handling impossible — a catch block cannot distinguish 'user passed wrong metric to raise()' from 'metric node has a bad signature string'. This will be a concrete problem in v0.3.5 when the mathjs backend needs to branch on error type.
findings.suggested_fix: Introduce distinct error subclasses: `MetricIndexVarianceError` for mixed-variance metric indices, `MetricSignatureFormatError` for malformed signature strings, and `RaiseLowerMetricVarianceError` for the raise/lower variance mismatch. Update §VIII.2 and §VIII.5 accordingly. The existing `MetricSignatureError` name can be retired or kept as a base class.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE: raise-lower-fresh-label-deterministic is underspecified — 'deterministic' without a seed is not reproducible across library versions
findings.description: The rule says the fresh-label scheme is 'implementation-defined' but 'MUST be deterministic so error messages and serialized ASTs are reproducible across runs'. Determinism within a single run is trivially achievable with a counter, but the rule does not say the scheme must be STABLE across library versions. If v0.3.5 changes the counter start or naming template (e.g., from `ν_1` to `__fresh_ν_0`), serialized ASTs from v0.3.0 will have different labels than those produced by v0.3.5 — breaking any consumer that stores or diffs ASTs. The spec should either (a) pin the naming scheme or (b) explicitly state that fresh labels are NOT part of the serialized public contract and must be stripped before storage.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a clause: 'Fresh labels produced by alpha-conversion are NOT part of the public AST contract. Serialized forms intended for cross-version storage MUST use the `raise()`/`lower()` call-site representation, not the expanded tensor-product. Alternatively, pin the naming scheme as `<original-label>_<zero-based-counter>` and commit to it as a SemVer-minor-stable detail.'

findings.title: §VIII.8 worked example: `contract()` called with three arguments but the v0.2.0 contract signature is binary
findings.location: §VIII.8, line `export const BE37_EIKONAL_LHS = contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S, dnu_S);`
findings.description: The spec's own §VIII.8 calls `contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S, dnu_S)` with three operands. The v0.2.0 `contract()` function (referenced as the existing path in §VIII.5 rule raise-lower-construct-tensor-product) is a binary operation on two tensor-product operands. The spec never defines a variadic `contract()` overload in v0.3.0. If `contract()` remains binary, the example is wrong and would need to be `contract(contract(g_inverse_eikonal, dmu_S), dnu_S)` or similar. If `contract()` is being extended to variadic in v0.3.0, that extension must be specified — it is a new API surface that affects SemVer and the §VIII.11 additive-only claim.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) rewrite the example to use nested binary `contract()` calls and add a note explaining the associativity, or (b) add a §VIII.X section specifying the variadic `contract(...operands)` overload, its left-associative semantics, and update §VIII.11 to list it as a new API addition.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE: pderiv-rank-equals-of-rank-plus-one is silent on rank of `of` when `of` is itself a tensor-partial-derivative
findings.description: The rule states 'If `of` is rank-N, the resulting expression is rank-(N+1)'. It does not address what 'rank' means when `of` is itself a `tensor-partial-derivative` node (a nested second-order partial derivative). The rank of a `tensor-partial-derivative` node is not defined anywhere in §VIII — only the rank of `metric-tensor` (2), `kronecker-delta` (2), and `tensor-symbol` (length of its index list) are implied. Without a recursive rank definition, the rule is incomplete and an implementation of second-order derivatives (needed for the wave operator in v0.4.0) has no spec to follow.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to pderiv-rank-equals-of-rank-plus-one: 'The rank of a `tensor-partial-derivative` node is defined recursively as `rank(of) + 1`. This definition applies when `of` is itself a `tensor-partial-derivative`, enabling second-order and higher partial derivatives.'

findings.title: §VIII.1 Grammar: Signature production rule accepts a single sign without a comma, making '+' and '-' ambiguous with a 1-entry signature
findings.description: The grammar reads `Signature ::= "+" | "-" (",(" "+" | "-"))*`. The outer alternation `"+" | "-"` matches a bare `+` or `-` as a complete signature (1-dimensional space). The second alternative `"-" (",(" "+" | "-"))*` also matches a bare `-`. This means a 1-entry signature is syntactically valid, but the rule in §VIII.2 (metric-tensor-signature-required) says an empty signature is rejected — it says nothing about a 1-entry signature for a rank-2 metric. A rank-2 metric with a 1-entry signature is physically nonsensical (the signature length should equal the manifold dimension, which for a rank-2 metric is implied by the index range). The grammar should either enforce signature length = manifold dimension or the spec should explicitly state that signature length validation is deferred to v0.3.5.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a note under metric-tensor-signature-required: 'v0.3.0 does not enforce that signature length equals the manifold dimension (that constraint requires a dimension parameter not present in v0.3.0). A signature with at least one entry is accepted. The mathjs backend (v0.3.5) will enforce signature-length = matrix dimension.' Also fix the grammar ambiguity by using `("+" | "-") ("," ("+" | "-"))*` to make the structure unambiguous.

findings.title: §VIII.9 preview test for `∂_μ g_νλ` is specified but the rule does not address index-label collision between wrtIndex and g_lower's own indices
findings.description: §VIII.9 states `pderiv(g_lower, x_coord, {label: 'μ', variance: 'lower'})` produces free indices `{μ:lower, ν:lower, λ:lower}` assuming `g_lower` had labels ν, λ. The collision rule in §VIII.4 (pderiv-label-collision-rejected) says: 'If `wrtIndex.label` collides with an existing free index in `of`'s free-indices map, the expression is rejected.' For the Christoffel symbol, the user will write `pderiv(g_lower, x_coord, {label: 'ν', variance: 'lower'})` where `g_lower` has labels ν and λ — this COLLIDES with ν in g_lower's free indices and would be rejected. But the Christoffel formula requires exactly this: `∂_ν g_ρμ`. The spec's collision rule as written makes the Christoffel building block impossible to construct without renaming g_lower's indices first. This is a forward-compat blocker for v0.4.0.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) require the user to alpha-rename `g_lower`'s indices before calling `pderiv` (document this in §VIII.9 with an example), or (b) specify that `pderiv` performs automatic alpha-conversion on `of`'s indices when a collision is detected (analogous to raise/lower), or (c) clarify that the collision rule only applies to the RESULT's free-index map and that the user is responsible for choosing non-colliding labels. Option (a) is safest for v0.3.0; document it explicitly in §VIII.9.

findings.title: §VIII.10 BREAKING flag does not address tensor-partial-derivative's dim field in the v0.5.0 refactor
findings.description: §VIII.10 lists `metric-tensor`, `tensor-symbol`, and `kronecker-delta` as participants in the v0.5.0 `dim: Dimension | DimensionMatrix` refactor. `tensor-partial-derivative` is omitted. But `tensor-partial-derivative` also has an output dim (computed as `divide(of.dim, wrt.dim)`). If `of` is a Faraday tensor with heterogeneous component dims in v0.5.0, the output dim of `pderiv(F, x, ...)` is also heterogeneous. Omitting `tensor-partial-derivative` from the BREAKING flag means the v0.5.0 design pass will encounter an unscoped refactor.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `tensor-partial-derivative` to the list of node kinds in §VIII.10 that participate in the v0.5.0 dim refactor. Note that its output dim computation rule (pderiv-dim-divides-by-wrt-dim) will need to be generalized to `DimensionMatrix / Dimension` or `DimensionMatrix / DimensionMatrix`.

findings.title: §VIII.7 _origin provenance marker stripped on JSON serialization — but no round-trip spec exists
findings.description: The spec says the `_origin?: 'raise' | 'lower'` field 'gets stripped on JSON serialization'. There is no spec for what happens when a serialized AST is deserialized and then passed back to `raise()`/`lower()` — the provenance is lost, so the error message quality degrades silently. More critically, if v0.3.5's mathjs backend serializes and deserializes ASTs as part of its evaluation pipeline, the provenance loss is invisible to the user. The spec should either (a) define a round-trip contract that preserves provenance, or (b) explicitly state that provenance is ephemeral and error-message quality after deserialization is best-effort.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a note: 'The `_origin` marker is ephemeral and is NOT preserved across serialization/deserialization. Error messages for `IndexLabelCollisionError` after deserialization will not include raise/lower context. This is acceptable for v0.3.0; v0.3.5 should evaluate whether to include provenance in the serialized form as an optional debug field.'

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE: raise-requires-label-present-in-operand does not specify the error type for 'already upper' case
findings.description: The rule says 'If `label` is absent from operand's free indices or already upper, the helper rejects with a descriptive error.' It names no error class. The five new error subclasses listed in §VIII.11 do not include one for this case. An implementor has no guidance on whether to throw a new error, reuse `VarianceMismatchError`, or use a generic `TypeError`. This will produce inconsistent implementations and makes programmatic error handling impossible.
findings.suggested_fix: Name a specific error class, e.g., `RaiseLowerLabelError`, and add it to the §VIII.11 error-subclass list. Specify two distinct messages: one for 'label not found in operand free indices' and one for 'label found but already has upper variance'.

findings.title: §VIII.3 kronecker-delta-dim-default-dimensionless: `kronecker()` helper is referenced but never declared
findings.description: The rule mentions a `kronecker()` helper that 'defaults to DIMENSIONLESS when omitted'. No such helper is declared in §VIII.1's grammar, §VIII.5's helper contract, or §VIII.11's new-module list. The `metric.ts` module is listed as new, but it is unclear whether `kronecker()` lives there. This is a dangling reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a §VIII.X (or subsection of §VIII.5) specifying the `kronecker(label_upper, label_lower, dim?)` helper signature, its return type (`kronecker-delta` node), and that it lives in `src/dimensional/metric.ts`.

findings.title: §VIII.4 pderiv-role-inherits-from-of cites 'Design §13 Q1 locked decision' with no accessible reference
findings.description: The rule ends with '(Per Design §13 Q1 locked decision.)' This is an opaque internal reference. Readers of the spec cannot verify the rationale, and future maintainers cannot find the decision record. The spec should either inline the rationale or provide a resolvable path (e.g., `docs/planning/design-decisions.md#q1`).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace '(Per Design §13 Q1 locked decision.)' with a resolvable reference such as '(Rationale: `docs/planning/design-decisions.md#metric-layer-q1-role-inheritance`.)' and ensure that document exists.

findings.title: §VIII.8 dimensional trace claims pderiv output is DIMENSIONLESS but the rule says divide(LENGTH, LENGTH)
findings.description: The trace says '`pderiv(S, x_coord, ...)` produces dim `divide(LENGTH, LENGTH) = DIMENSIONLESS`'. This is correct arithmetic but the spec should explicitly note that this equality (`divide(LENGTH, LENGTH) = DIMENSIONLESS`) is a property of the Dimension algebra, not an assumption. If the Dimension type uses structural equality rather than dimensional reduction, `divide(LENGTH, LENGTH)` might not equal `DIMENSIONLESS` without a simplification step. The spec should clarify whether the Dimension algebra auto-simplifies.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a parenthetical: '(assuming the Dimension algebra reduces `divide(LENGTH, LENGTH)` to `DIMENSIONLESS` — see Part II §X for the simplification rules)'. If no such section exists, add a note that auto-simplification is required for this trace to hold.

findings.title: No test specified for the MetricSignatureError / malformed-signature path
findings.description: §VIII.8 references `tests/bridges/be-37-shapiro-eikonal-structural.test.ts` and `tests/dimensional/raise-lower.test.ts`. §VIII.9 references `tests/dimensional/covariant-derivative-preview.test.ts`. No test file is specified for the metric-tensor validation error paths: malformed signature string, empty signature, mixed-variance metric indices (`MetricSignatureError`), or invalid metric rank (`InvalidMetricRankError`). These are the primary guard rails of the metric-tensor node and their absence from the test spec is a gap.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a §VIII.X (or a note in §VIII.2) specifying `tests/dimensional/metric-tensor-validation.test.ts` covering: (a) empty signature rejected, (b) non-+/- signature entry rejected, (c) mixed-variance indices rejected, (d) rank-0 rejected, (e) rank-3 rejected. Each test should assert the specific error class thrown.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE: raise-lower-internal-alpha-conversion has no specified test for the collision-avoidance property
findings.description: §VIII.8 says `tests/dimensional/raise-lower.test.ts` 'exercises the renaming/contraction interplay in dedicated unit tests' but gives no detail on what cases are covered. The critical invariant — that the fresh label does NOT collide with any free index in `operand` — is not specified as a named test case. An implementation could pass a trivial test (no collision in the happy path) while failing when `operand` has an index that happens to match the naive fresh-label scheme.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to §VIII.5 or a test-spec appendix: 'The raise-lower test suite MUST include a case where `operand` already has a free index whose label matches the naive fresh-label candidate (e.g., `ν_1`), verifying that the generator increments to `ν_2` or equivalent to avoid collision.'

strengths: The scope boundary (v0.3.0 vs v0.4.0 vs v0.5.0) is exceptionally clear — Christoffel symbols, covariant derivatives, and Faraday-style heterogeneous-dim tensors are each explicitly deferred with rationale.

The BREAKING CHANGE flag in §VIII.10 is proactive and correctly identifies all three node kinds affected by the uniform-component-dim assumption, giving the v0.5.0 design pass a concrete starting constraint.

The §VIII.8 worked example is unusually thorough: it includes a dimensional trace, explains the raise-vs-direct-contract trade-off with a concrete failure mode (the alpha-converted label not matching dnu_S's ν), and cross-references the relevant test files.
The SemVer posture in §VIII.11 is precise — it correctly identifies that error message text is not part of the SemVer contract while flagging the two messages that changed.
TENSOR-RULE tags are machine-parseable and consistently applied across all six invariant sections, enabling automated rule extraction.
The §VIII.7 provenance marker design (`_origin?: 'raise' | 'lower'`) correctly isolates internal implementation detail from the public ExprNode contract by specifying JSON-serialization stripping.

The forward-compat note in §VIII.9 that `∂_μ S = ∇_μ S` for scalars (Christoffel terms cancel) is a correct and useful observation that will prevent unnecessary v0.4.0 migration churn for scalar-field equations.

summary: The test suite covers the main happy-path and error-path branches for MetricTensorNode validation, but contains several correctness gaps: the wrong error class is expected for the duplicate-label case, a critical mixed-variance case is mis-classified, and the freeIndices shape contract is never verified for the contravariant path's dimension. Forward-compat coverage for v0.4.0 Christoffel/covariant-derivative consumers is absent.

findings.title: Duplicate-label test expects MetricSignatureError but should expect a distinct DuplicateIndexError (or the wrong rule is being tested)
findings.description: The test 'rejects duplicate label within metric (e.g., g_μμ)' asserts `toThrow(MetricSignatureError)`. Duplicate index labels within a single tensor are a structural/index-algebra violation, not a signature-format violation. If the validator actually throws `MetricSignatureError` for this case it is mis-classifying the error (conflating two distinct TENSOR-RULEs), which will silently mask a missing `DuplicateIndexError` class. If a `DuplicateIndexError` is (or will be) introduced in v0.3.5/v0.4.0, this test will start failing with a misleading message. The test name says 'duplicate label' but the assertion says 'signature error' — one of them is wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) introduce and import `DuplicateIndexError` from `errors.ts` and change the assertion to `toThrow(DuplicateIndexError)`, or (b) if the design decision is to reuse `MetricSignatureError`, add an explicit comment in both the test and the error class documenting that choice, and add a `.message` assertion to confirm the right code path fired: `expect(() => validate(bad)).toThrow(MetricSignatureError); // code: DUPLICATE_INDEX`

findings.title: Mixed-variance test expects MetricSignatureError — wrong error class per TENSOR-RULE metric-tensor-indices-same-variance
findings.description: TENSOR-RULE `metric-tensor-indices-same-variance` is a structural index rule, not a signature-format rule. Throwing `MetricSignatureError` for a mixed-variance metric conflates two independent invariants. If the validator is later refactored to throw a dedicated `MetricVarianceError` (a natural step before v0.4.0 raise/lower work), this test will fail. More importantly, if the validator currently throws `MetricSignatureError` for *both* bad-signature and bad-variance inputs, a regression that swaps the two code paths would go undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Introduce `MetricVarianceError` in `errors.ts` (or reuse `InvalidMetricRankError` with a different code), import it here, and assert `toThrow(MetricVarianceError)`. At minimum add a `.message` snapshot: `expect(() => validate(bad)).toThrow(/same-variance/i)`.

findings.title: freeIndices contract not verified for contravariant metric — inferredDimension also unchecked
findings.description: The 'validates a well-formed contravariant metric (both upper)' test checks `freeIndices` counts but never asserts `result.ok === true` or `result.inferredDimension`. If `validate` returns `ok: false` with a non-throwing error path, the freeIndices assertions would still pass while the validation itself failed silently. This is inconsistent with the covariant test which checks all three.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(result.ok).toBe(true);` and `expect(result.inferredDimension).toEqual(DIMENSIONLESS);` to the contravariant test, mirroring the covariant test structure.

findings.title: No test for rank-0 metric (empty indices array)
findings.description: The rank-rejection tests cover rank-1 and rank-3 but not rank-0 (empty `indices: []`). A validator that checks `indices.length !== 2` would catch this, but a validator that checks `indices.length > 2 || indices.length < 1` would silently accept it. This edge case is cheap to add and guards against off-by-one bugs in the rank check.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `it('rejects rank-0 metric with InvalidMetricRankError', () => { const bad: MetricTensorNode = { kind: 'metric-tensor', name: 'g', indices: [], signature: '+,-,-,-', dim: DIMENSIONLESS }; expect(() => validate(bad)).toThrow(InvalidMetricRankError); });`

findings.title: No test for missing/undefined signature field
findings.description: The signature tests cover empty string and malformed string, but not `signature: undefined` (or the field being absent). TypeScript's type system prevents this at compile time, but at runtime (e.g., JSON deserialization from a mathjs backend in v0.3.5) the field could be missing. The validator should throw `MetricSignatureError` in that case; there is no test asserting it does.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `it('rejects undefined signature with MetricSignatureError', () => { const bad = { kind: 'metric-tensor', name: 'g', indices: [{ label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }, { label: 'ν', variance: 'lower' }], dim: DIMENSIONLESS } as unknown as MetricTensorNode; expect(() => validate(bad)).toThrow(MetricSignatureError); });`

findings.title: freeIndices.size is never checked for the contravariant metric
findings.description: The covariant test asserts `result.freeIndices.size === 2`, but the contravariant test skips this check. If a bug caused the contravariant path to return an empty or oversized map, the test would not catch it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(result.freeIndices.size).toBe(2);` before the per-label assertions in the contravariant test.

findings.title: No test exercises the TENSOR-RULE metric-tensor-dim-user-specified with a zero-dimension (e.g., TIME²)
findings.description: The `allows user-specified non-DIMENSIONLESS dim` test only checks `L:2`. There is no test for a dimension with negative exponents (e.g., `T:-2`) or a mixed dimension, which are valid for curved-spacetime line-element metrics. This matters for v0.4.0 Christoffel symbols where the metric dimension propagates into derivative terms.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test with `dim: { L: 0, M: 0, T: -2, I: 0, Theta: 0, N: 0, J: 0 }` and assert `result.inferredDimension` equals that value.

findings.title: No test verifies that freeIndices entries are stable across alpha-conversion (raise/lower helpers)
findings.description: v0.3.0 adds raise/lower helpers with internal alpha-conversion. The freeIndices map returned by `validate(g_lower)` will be consumed by those helpers. There is no test asserting that the map's label strings survive a round-trip through alpha-conversion (i.e., that the labels are canonical, not renamed). Without this, a subtle alpha-conversion bug could produce wrong contractions in v0.4.0 covariant derivatives.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an integration-style test that calls `raiseIndex(g_lower, 'μ')` (or equivalent) and asserts the resulting node's freeIndices still contains `'μ'` with `{ upper: 1, lower: 0 }`, confirming the label is preserved or correctly renamed.

findings.title: Shared fixture nodes (g_lower, g_upper) are declared at describe-scope without Object.freeze — mutation in one test could affect others
findings.description: Both `g_lower` and `g_upper` are `const` references but their contents are mutable objects. If `validate` (or a future helper) mutates the node in-place (e.g., attaches inferred metadata), later tests in the same describe block would see the mutated state. This is a latent ordering-dependency bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap fixtures with `Object.freeze` recursively, or move them inside individual `it` blocks, or use a `beforeEach` factory: `const makeGLower = (): MetricTensorNode => ({ ... })`.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE comments at top of describe block are not linked to individual tests
findings.description: The five TENSOR-RULE tags are listed once at the describe level. It is not clear which `it` block exercises which rule. `metric-tensor-free-indices-from-decl` in particular has no obviously corresponding test (the freeIndices assertions are spread across two tests without labeling).
findings.suggested_fix: Move each TENSOR-RULE comment to the `it` block that primarily exercises it, e.g., `// TENSOR-RULE: metric-tensor-free-indices-from-decl` above the covariant validation test.

strengths: Happy-path tests for both covariant and contravariant forms are present and check the freeIndices shape contract (counts and per-label variance objects), not just `ok: true`.
Error-class assertions use `toThrow(SpecificErrorClass)` rather than string matching, which will catch class hierarchy regressions.
The `allows user-specified non-DIMENSIONLESS dim` test correctly validates TENSOR-RULE metric-tensor-dim-user-specified with a concrete non-trivial dimension object.
Rank boundary tests cover both under-rank (rank-1) and over-rank (rank-3), providing a bracket around the valid rank-2 constraint.
Imports are scoped correctly — `MetricTensorNode` is imported as a type-only import, keeping the test file free of runtime coupling to the validator internals.

summary: The test suite covers the three TENSOR-RULEs for Kronecker-delta validation reasonably well, but contains one semantically incorrect assertion, one missing coverage gap for a critical invariant, and a physically dubious test that may encode a wrong assumption about the library's intended contract.

findings.title: freeIndices assertions in 'lower-then-upper order' test check absolute labels, not positional order — but the real risk is the test silently passes even if variance is swapped
findings.description: The test named 'validates lower-then-upper order (δ_ν^μ)' asserts `result.freeIndices.get('μ')` equals `{ upper: 1, lower: 0 }` and `result.freeIndices.get('ν')` equals `{ upper: 0, lower: 1 }`. These are identical to the assertions in the canonical δ^μ_ν test. If the validator has a bug where it ignores the declared variance and always assigns upper to 'μ' and lower to 'ν' by label heuristic (e.g., alphabetical or Unicode order), this test would still pass. The test does not verify that the *first* index in the array (label 'ν', variance 'lower') is recorded as lower, nor that the *second* index (label 'μ', variance 'upper') is recorded as upper — it only checks by label name, which happens to produce the same expected values as the canonical case. The test should instead assert on the labels that differ in position: specifically that 'ν' is upper=0/lower=1 and 'μ' is upper=1/lower=0, which it does — but it never checks that swapping the array order does NOT change the outcome, making it impossible to distinguish a correct implementation from a label-keyed lookup bug. A distinct pair of labels (e.g., 'α' upper / 'β' lower vs 'β' lower / 'α' upper) would expose this.

findings.title: No test for repeated-label (same label on both indices) Kronecker delta — contraction or error?
findings.description: TENSOR-RULE `kronecker-delta-free-indices-from-decl` implies that both indices become free. But δ^μ_μ (same label, mixed variance) is a valid Einstein contraction that traces to the spacetime dimension (e.g., 4 in 4D). The validator must decide: is `{ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }` a contraction (producing a scalar with no free indices) or an error? This case is entirely untested. For v0.4.0 Christoffel/covariant-derivative work, this distinction is load-bearing — g^μ_μ = n is used constantly. Without a test, the behavior is undefined and a silent regression is likely.

findings.title: 'allows user-specified non-DIMENSIONLESS dim' test encodes a physically incorrect contract
findings.description: The Kronecker delta δ^μ_ν is dimensionless by definition in all standard tensor calculus formulations — it is a pure index-selector with value 0 or 1. Allowing a user to override its dimension to `{ L: 1, ... }` and having `validate` return `ok: true` would mean the validator accepts a dimensionally inconsistent AST node. If this test reflects actual validator behavior, it is a semantic bug in the validator that this test is blessing. Even if the intent is 'the user knows what they are doing', the test name says 'rare but valid' with no citation.
