For v0.3.5 (mathjs numerical backend), a dimensioned Kronecker delta would produce wrong physical units in any contraction. The test should either be removed, or if the override is intentional (e.g., for weighted Kronecker in non-standard bases), it must be gated behind an explicit `allowDimensionOverride: true` flag and the test must assert that the default path rejects it.

findings.title: No test for rank-0 (empty indices array) Kronecker delta
findings.description: The rank tests cover rank-1 and rank-3 but not rank-0 (empty `indices: []`). An empty array is a distinct edge case from a single-element array — some validators short-circuit on `length === 0` before checking the mixed-variance rule, potentially throwing the wrong error type or no error at all. TENSOR-RULE `kronecker-delta-rank-2-only` should cover this, but it is not verified.

findings.title: freeIndices count assertion uses `.size` but never verifies the exact set of keys
findings.description: The canonical test asserts `result.freeIndices.size === 2` and then checks two specific keys. This is fine for the happy path, but if the validator accidentally inserts a third phantom key (e.g., an empty-string key from a parsing bug), `size` would be 3 and the test would fail — but only incidentally. More importantly, the test does not assert that *only* 'μ' and 'ν' are present. For a Map, `expect([...result.freeIndices.keys()].sort()).toEqual(['μ', 'ν'].sort())` is a stronger and clearer assertion. This becomes important for v0.4.0 where free-index sets are composed across Christoffel terms.
findings.suggested_fix:
```typescript
expect([...result.freeIndices.keys()].sort()).toEqual(['μ', 'ν'].sort());
```
Replace or supplement the `.size` check with this in both the canonical and reversed-order tests.

findings.title: No test exercises validate() return type shape for use by raise/lower helpers
findings.description: The v0.3.0 release notes mention raise/lower helpers with internal alpha-conversion that consume the validator's output. The tests only check `result.ok`, `result.inferredDimension`, and `result.freeIndices`. If the validator result also carries a `contractedIndices` field (needed by raise/lower to know which indices were consumed), that field is never asserted here. A missing or wrongly-typed `contractedIndices` on a Kronecker delta result would silently break raise/lower in v0.3.5.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add an assertion in the canonical test:
```typescript
expect(result.contractedIndices).toBeDefined();
expect(result.contractedIndices.size).toBe(0); // no contraction on δ^μ_ν
```
Adjust field name to match the actual validator return type.

strengths: All three TENSOR-RULEs cited in the describe-block header are exercised by at least one test, providing clear traceability between spec rules and test cases.

Error-type specificity is correctly tested — both `InvalidKroneckerRankError` and `KroneckerVarianceError` are asserted by class, not just by message string, which will catch accidental error-type regressions.
The shared `delta_μν` fixture at describe scope is reused correctly and is not mutated between tests, avoiding cross-test contamination.
Both both-upper and both-lower variance violations are independently tested, ruling out an implementation that only checks one ordering.
The test file imports from the correct v0.3.0 module paths (`metric-validators.js`) rather than legacy paths, confirming the import surface is intentional.

summary: The test file covers the seven TENSOR-RULEs listed in its header comment reasonably well, but several tests have correctness gaps: the 'ignores wrt own free indices' test is a duplicate of the first test rather than an independent probe, the 'inherits role' test asserts nothing about role inheritance, and the nested-pderiv test reuses the same `wrt` symbol for both derivatives without verifying the dimension formula is actually L²-based. One critical gap is that no test exercises the `pderiv-free-indices-union` rule when `of` already carries multiple free indices.

findings.title: 'ignores wrt own free indices' test is structurally identical to the first test and does not independently verify the rule
findings.description: The test named 'ignores wrt own free indices (per Part-VIII §VIII.4)' constructs exactly the same `phi`, `x`, and `dPhi` nodes as the first test ('infers dim = divide(of.dim, wrt.dim) for scalar of'). It only checks `freeIndices.has('α') === false` and `freeIndices.has('μ') === true`, both of which are already implied by the first test's assertions. The rule it is supposed to verify — that `wrt`'s own free indices are NOT propagated into the result — would only be meaningfully tested if the validator could plausibly propagate them (e.g., by using a `wrt` symbol whose free index label does NOT appear in `wrtIndex`, and then confirming the result map has exactly one entry). As written, the test cannot distinguish a correct implementation from one that accidentally propagates `α` but then the first test catches it, or from one that never propagates anything at all.

findings.title: 'inherits role from of' test makes no assertion about role inheritance
findings.description: The test is named 'inherits role from of when of is a tensor-symbol with role' and the TENSOR-RULE `pderiv-role-inherits-from-of` is listed in the header. The test body only asserts `result.ok === true`, which is already covered by the first test. The comment 'validator doesn't expose it on ValidationResult' suggests the rule is untestable at this layer, but that means the rule is unverified in v0.3.0. If `ValidationResult` genuinely cannot surface role, the test should either be marked `.todo` / `.skip` with an explicit reason, or `ValidationResult` should be extended to expose `inferredRole` so the invariant can be checked. Leaving a passing test that asserts nothing about the named rule creates false confidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Option A — if `ValidationResult` can be extended: add `inferredRole?: string` to the result type and assert `expect(result.inferredRole).toBe('field')`. Option B — if role is intentionally deferred to v0.4.0: replace the test body with `it.todo('pderiv-role-inherits-from-of: deferred to v0.4.0 covariant-derivative work')` so CI does not silently pass an unverified invariant.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE `pderiv-free-indices-union` is not independently tested for the multi-index case
findings.description: The header lists `pderiv-free-indices-union` as a rule under test, but no test constructs an `of` node with two or more free indices and verifies that all of them appear in the result alongside the new `wrtIndex`. The rank-2 test ('increases rank by 1') only checks a rank-1 `of` with a single free index `ν`. A validator bug that drops all but the first free index from `of` would pass every existing test.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test with a rank-2 `of` (e.g., `F = tsym('F', [{label:'ν', variance:'upper'}, {label:'ρ', variance:'upper'}], POTENTIAL)`) and assert `result.freeIndices.size === 3` with correct entries for `μ`, `ν`, and `ρ`.

findings.title: Nested pderiv test reuses the same `wrt` symbol for both derivatives without asserting dimension is `POTENTIAL / LENGTH²`
findings.description: The test comment says 'dim should be POTENTIAL / LENGTH²' and calls `divide(divide(POTENTIAL, LENGTH), LENGTH)`, which is correct in intent. However, the assertion relies on referential equality of the dimension objects returned by `divide`. If `divide` returns a new object each call (likely), `toEqual` performs deep equality — which is fine — but the test does not verify the numeric exponents explicitly. More importantly, the test does not assert `result.freeIndices.size === 2` before checking individual entries, so a result with extra spurious indices (e.g., `α` leaking from `wrt`) would still pass the two `get` assertions. This is a weak assertion set for a compound node.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add `expect(result.freeIndices.size).toBe(2)` before the individual `get` checks (already present — good), but also add an explicit dimension check against known exponents:
```typescript
const dim = result.inferredDimension;
expect(dim.L).toBe(POTENTIAL.L - 2 * LENGTH.L); // 2 - 2 = 0
expect(dim.M).toBe(POTENTIAL.M);                 // 1
expect(dim.T).toBe(POTENTIAL.T);                 // -3
expect(dim.I).toBe(POTENTIAL.I);                 // -1
```
This makes the test robust to a `divide` implementation that returns a structurally correct but numerically wrong object.

findings.title: No test for `pderiv-label-collision-rejected` when collision is between `wrtIndex` and a free index inherited from a nested `of` (not the immediate `of`)
findings.description: The existing collision test only checks a direct collision between `wrtIndex.label` and the immediate `of`'s free index. The `pderiv-free-indices-union` rule implies that free indices from deeply nested `of` nodes are also in scope. A validator that only checks the immediate `of.freeIndices` and not the full union would miss a collision introduced at a deeper level. This is especially relevant for the nested-pderiv case.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test where `of` is itself a `TensorPartialDerivativeNode` whose result carries free index `μ`, and the outer `wrtIndex` is also `μ:lower`. Expect `IndexLabelCollisionError` to be thrown.

findings.title: Type-cast `'upper' as 'lower'` in the rejection test silently defeats TypeScript's variance check
findings.description: `wrtIndex: { label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' as 'lower' }` uses a type assertion to smuggle an invalid value past the type system. This means if the `TensorPartialDerivativeNode` type is later tightened to a discriminated union that makes `variance: 'upper'` a compile-time error on `wrtIndex`, this test will silently stop compiling rather than failing at runtime as intended. It also hides the fact that the type system itself does not enforce the lower-only constraint.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `as unknown as TensorPartialDerivativeNode` on the whole node object, or cast only the `wrtIndex` field via `as { label: string; variance: 'lower' }` with a comment explaining the intentional type violation. Better: add a separate type-level test (using `@ts-expect-error`) that confirms `variance: 'upper'` is rejected by the type system if the type is ever tightened.

findings.title: `TensorPartialDerivativeNode` is imported from `metric-validators` rather than a canonical types module
findings.description: The import `import type { TensorPartialDerivativeNode } from '../../src/dimensional/metric-validators.js'` couples the test to an implementation file. If the type is moved to `types.ts` or a dedicated `ast.ts` in v0.3.5/v0.4.0, this import will break. The type should be re-exported from the public surface (`types.ts` or `index.ts`) and tests should import from there.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-export `TensorPartialDerivativeNode` from `src/dimensional/types.ts` (or `src/dimensional/index.ts`) and update the import to `import type { TensorPartialDerivativeNode } from '../../src/dimensional/types.js'`.

strengths: All seven TENSOR-RULEs listed in the header comment have at least a nominal test, providing a clear traceability matrix between spec rules and test cases.
The `freeIndices` shape assertions (`{ upper: N, lower: N }`) are precise and would catch variance-tracking bugs, not just label-presence bugs.
The nested second-derivative test is a valuable compound case that exercises recursive validation and dimension accumulation in a single assertion block.
Using `tsym` with explicit `role` arguments in the role-inheritance test correctly sets up the precondition even if the postcondition assertion is currently weak.
The `PartialDerivativeIndexVarianceError` and `IndexLabelCollisionError` rejection tests use typed error classes rather than message-string matching, making them robust to error message rewording.

summary: Five smoke tests verify that v0.3.0 error subclasses are instantiable and carry the right fields. The tests are structurally sound but contain several gaps that leave real invariants unverified and will silently pass even if the implementation is subtly broken.

findings.title: MetricSignatureError message assertion tests the wrong string
findings.description: The test constructs the error with reason `'mixed-variance indices not allowed'` and then asserts `err.message.toContain('mixed-variance')`. This passes trivially if the implementation simply interpolates `err.reason` into the message. However, the test never checks that the reason string itself is actually embedded — it checks a substring of the reason. If the implementation hard-codes the word 'mixed-variance' in the message template but ignores `reason` entirely, the assertion still passes. The `err.reason` field is verified separately, but the message/reason linkage is never proven.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(err.message).toContain(err.reason)` (or the full reason string) so the test proves the reason is interpolated into the message, not just that the message contains an overlapping substring.

findings.title: No test for the 'lower' variance path of KroneckerVarianceError
findings.description: Only `'upper'` is exercised. The Kronecker delta must reject both `(upper, upper)` and `(lower, lower)` pairs. If the implementation special-cases `'upper'` (e.g. a typo in a switch/if), the `'lower'` path is silently broken. This is especially important for forward-compat with v0.4.0 covariant-derivative logic that will rely on both variance checks.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a second `it` block (or a parameterised test) that constructs `new KroneckerVarianceError('lower')` and asserts `err.bothVariance === 'lower'` and `err.message.toContain('lower')`.

findings.title: PartialDerivativeIndexVarianceError is never tested for the 'upper' guard path — only the error object itself
findings.description: The test only checks that the error class can be constructed with a label and that the message contains 'lower'. It does not verify that the validator which *throws* this error actually throws it when given an upper index. The class constructor test is necessary but not sufficient; the throwing site (the partial-derivative AST node or its validator) is completely untested here. A future refactor could rename the throwing site without breaking this test.
findings.suggested_fix: Import the partial-derivative validator/factory (e.g. `createPartialDerivativeNode` or `validatePartialDerivativeIndex`) and add a test: `expect(() => createPartialDerivativeNode({ wrtIndex: { label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' } })).toThrow(PartialDerivativeIndexVarianceError)`. Keep the constructor test as-is.

findings.title: InvalidMetricRankError does not test the rank-1 or rank-0 boundary, only rank-3
findings.description: Only `actualRank = 3` is exercised. Rank 0 and rank 1 are equally invalid and are the more common accidental inputs (e.g. passing a scalar or vector where a metric is expected). An off-by-one in the rank guard (`rank < 2` vs `rank !== 2`) would not be caught.
findings.suggested_fix: Parameterise the test over `[0, 1, 3, 4]` using `it.each` and assert that each produces an `InvalidMetricRankError` with the correct `actualRank`.

findings.title: No test that error subclasses preserve stack traces (instanceof chain through Error)
findings.description: Every test checks `instanceof Error` and `instanceof UPTError`, but none checks `err.stack !== undefined`. In environments where `Error.captureStackTrace` is absent or where the subclass forgets to call `super(message)` before setting `this.name`, the stack can be missing. This is a runtime-debuggability regression that is invisible to the current assertions.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(err.stack).toBeDefined()` to at least one representative test (e.g. `InvalidMetricRankError`). Vitest runs in Node where `stack` is always populated when `super()` is called correctly, so a missing `super()` call will surface immediately.

findings.title: InvalidKroneckerRankError message is only checked for 'Kronecker', not for the actual rank value
findings.description: `err.message.toContain('Kronecker')` is asserted but the actual rank (3) is never checked to appear in the message. A message like `'Kronecker delta must be rank-2'` passes the test even if `actualRank` is never interpolated, making the message useless for debugging.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(err.message).toContain('3')` (or `String(err.actualRank)`) to verify the offending rank is surfaced in the message.

findings.title: KroneckerVarianceError property is named `bothVariance` — semantically ambiguous for a mixed-variance future extension
findings.description: The test asserts `err.bothVariance === 'upper'`, implying the property name is `bothVariance`. This name is fine for v0.3.0 but will become confusing in v0.4.0 when the Christoffel/covariant-derivative layer may need to distinguish 'both upper' from 'both lower'. A name like `repeatedVariance` or `invalidVariance` is more forward-compatible. This is a test-driven signal about the underlying API name.
findings.suggested_fix: Consider renaming the property to `repeatedVariance` in the error class and updating this test accordingly before v0.3.5 locks the public API.

strengths: Every error subclass is verified to satisfy the full instanceof chain (Error → UPTError → concrete class), which catches broken super() calls or missing prototype fixups.
The `err.name` property is explicitly checked for each subclass, ensuring the name is set on the instance rather than inherited from Error.prototype.
Domain-specific context fields (tensorName, actualRank, reason, label, bothVariance) are all individually asserted, not just the message string.
Tests are isolated — each error is constructed independently with no shared state, making failures easy to localise.
Import structure is clean: all six error classes are imported from a single barrel path, which will make a future rename/move straightforward.

summary: The test file covers the happy-path construction of all three v0.3.0 AST node helpers, but it is shallow: it never validates index variance constraints, dimensional arithmetic, or any error path, leaving the most failure-prone invariants completely untested.

findings.title: metric() variance constraint never tested — both indices must be 'lower' (covariant) for a metric tensor
findings.description: The single metric() test only checks that the node is constructed when both indices are 'lower'. There is no test asserting that metric() throws (or returns an error node) when an 'upper' index is supplied. If the implementation silently accepts upper indices, downstream raise/lower helpers and the v0.4.0 Christoffel-symbol builder will silently produce malformed ASTs. The TENSOR-RULE invariant that g_{μν} must carry two covariant indices is a load-bearing contract for the entire metric layer.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: it('throws when an upper index is supplied', () => { expect(() => metric('g', [{ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }, { label: 'ν', variance: 'lower' }], DIMENSIONLESS, '+,-,-,-')).toThrow(/covariant|lower/i); });

findings.title: kronecker() variance constraint never tested — upper+lower pairing is the only valid form
findings.description: δ^μ_ν is only valid with one upper and one lower index. The tests confirm the happy path but never assert that kronecker('μ', 'ν') with swapped or identical variances is rejected. The 'accepts explicit dim override' test also does not re-check the index variances after the override, so a regression where dim override accidentally resets index variance would go undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test: it('throws when both indices have the same variance', () => { expect(() => kronecker('μ', 'ν', DIMENSIONLESS, 'lower', 'lower')).toThrow(); }); Also add expect(delta.indices[0]).toEqual({ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }) inside the 'accepts explicit dim override' test.

findings.title: pderiv() wrtIndex variance is never validated — must be 'lower' (∂/∂x^μ lowers the free index)
findings.description: The single pderiv() test passes { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' } which is correct, but there is no test asserting that passing variance: 'upper' is rejected. A partial derivative with respect to a contravariant coordinate produces an upper free index, which is the opposite of the standard convention (∂_μ). If the helper silently accepts 'upper', the v0.4.0 covariant-derivative builder will inherit the wrong index type.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: it('throws when wrtIndex variance is upper', () => { expect(() => pderiv(phi, x, { label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' })).toThrow(/lower|covariant/i); });

findings.title: Dimensional arithmetic of pderiv() output is never checked
findings.description: ∂φ/∂x^μ should carry dimension [φ] / [x] = DIMENSIONLESS / LENGTH = LENGTH^{-1}. The test constructs phi (DIMENSIONLESS) and x (LENGTH) but never asserts d.dim. If the implementation sets d.dim = phi.dim (a common copy-paste mistake), this test will not catch it, and every downstream equation that uses pderiv() will carry the wrong units.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: const INVERSE_LENGTH = { L: -1, M: 0, T: 0, I: 0, Theta: 0, N: 0, J: 0 }; expect(d.dim).toEqual(INVERSE_LENGTH);

findings.title: metric() signature field is not validated for format or consistency with index count
findings.description: The test passes '+,-,-,-' (4-component Minkowski signature) to a metric node that has only 2 indices. There is no assertion that the helper rejects a signature whose component count mismatches the index count, nor that malformed strings like '++--' or '' are rejected. This is a forward-compat risk: the v0.4.0 Christoffel builder will likely parse the signature to determine index raising/lowering signs.
findings.suggested_fix: Add tests: (1) expect(() => metric('g', twoIndices, DIMENSIONLESS, '+,-,-,-')).toThrow(/signature.*index/i) if mismatch should be an error, or document that signature is purely informational. (2) expect(() => metric('g', twoIndices, DIMENSIONLESS, 'invalid')).toThrow();

findings.title: No test for pderiv() when 'of' tensor has free indices — the index-set union is the critical path
findings.description: The only pderiv() test differentiates a scalar (phi with zero indices). The interesting and error-prone case is differentiating a tensor with existing free indices, e.g. ∂_μ A^ν, where the result must carry both ν (upper) and μ (lower) as free indices. This is the exact case the v0.4.0 covariant derivative will exercise. Testing only the scalar case gives false confidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: const A = tsym('A', [{ label: 'ν', variance: 'upper' }], LENGTH); const dA = pderiv(A, x, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }); expect(dA.indices).toEqual([{ label: 'ν', variance: 'upper' }, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }]);

findings.title: No test for pderiv() index collision (wrtIndex label already present in 'of' tensor)
findings.description: If pderiv(A^μ, x, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }) is called, the resulting node would have two indices labelled 'μ' with opposite variances — which is an implicit Einstein contraction, not a free index. The helper should either alpha-rename (the spec mentions internal alpha-conversion) or throw. This edge case is entirely untested.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: const B = tsym('B', [{ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }], LENGTH); expect(() => pderiv(B, x, { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' })).toThrow(/collision|alpha/i); — or, if alpha-conversion is the intended behaviour, assert that the output index label is renamed.

findings.title: kronecker() 'accepts explicit dim override' test does not assert anything meaningful about the override
findings.description: The test only checks delta.dim === LENGTH. It does not verify that the indices are still correctly set after the override, nor does it test that a physically nonsensical dim (e.g. LENGTH for a pure identity tensor) is either accepted with a warning or rejected. The test name implies a deliberate design decision but the test body does not document or enforce the rationale.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the test body: expect(delta.indices[0]).toEqual({ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }); expect(delta.indices[1]).toEqual({ label: 'ν', variance: 'lower' }); and add a comment explaining why a non-DIMENSIONLESS Kronecker delta is valid in this library.

findings.title: No test for metric() round-trip through raise/lower helpers — the primary consumer of metric nodes
findings.description: The v0.3.0 release notes cite raise/lower helpers with internal alpha-conversion as a key feature. The metric-helpers test file never exercises metric() as an argument to raise() or lower(). If the metric node's field names or structure differ from what raise/lower expect, the integration will fail at v0.3.5 or v0.4.0 rather than now.
findings.suggested_fix: Import raise and lower from the tensor module and add: it('metric node is accepted by raise() without throwing', () => { const g = metric(...); const A = tsym('A', [{ label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }], LENGTH); expect(() => raise(A, 'μ', g)).not.toThrow(); });

findings.title: LENGTH dimension object is defined inline in the test file rather than imported from a shared fixture
findings.description: const LENGTH = { L: 1, M: 0, T: 0, I: 0, Theta: 0, N: 0, J: 0 } is duplicated across test files. If the dimension object shape changes (e.g. adding a 'cd' candela field), every test file must be updated manually. A shared test-fixtures module would make this a single-point change.
findings.suggested_fix: Create tests/fixtures/dimensions.ts exporting LENGTH, MASS, TIME, etc., and import from there: import { LENGTH } from '../fixtures/dimensions.js';

strengths: All three v0.3.0 helper constructors (metric, kronecker, pderiv) are at least smoke-tested, ensuring the module exports are wired correctly.
The test correctly imports tsym to construct realistic tensor arguments for pderiv(), rather than using plain object literals, which means the test exercises the actual type boundary.
Index shape assertions use toEqual (deep equality) rather than toBe, which is correct for structural value objects.
DIMENSIONLESS is imported from the canonical types module rather than inlined, keeping the test aligned with the production type definition.

summary: The test suite covers the happy-path and several error-path scenarios for raise/lower with alpha-conversion, but contains two substantive correctness gaps: the error-type assertions for variance-mismatch cases are under-specified (only one of two checks the right exception class), and the 'already upper' rejection test does not verify the error is distinct from the 'label absent' error, making it impossible to tell whether the implementation is enforcing the right invariant. Additionally, the dimensional-consistency of the metric tensor is never validated, and the fresh-label collision test has a latent false-positive risk.

findings.title: 'rejects raise() when label is already upper in operand' does not assert error type
findings.description: The test `expect(() => raise(A_upper, g_inv, 'μ')).toThrow()` uses the bare `.toThrow()` matcher with no argument. This means any exception — including an unrelated runtime crash — will make the test pass. The TENSOR-RULE `raise-requires-label-present-in-operand` and the implicit rule that raise requires a lower-variance label are distinct invariants; the test cannot distinguish between them. Compare with the 'label absent' test immediately above, which also uses bare `.toThrow()`. If the implementation accidentally throws the 'label absent' error for the 'already upper' case (because it checks variance after presence), both tests still pass despite the wrong error being thrown.
findings.suggested_fix: Import and assert the specific error class, e.g. `import { RaiseVarianceError } from '../../src/dimensional/errors.js'` (or whatever the library exposes), then: `expect(() => raise(A_upper, g_inv, 'μ')).toThrow(RaiseVarianceError)`. If no dedicated class exists, at minimum assert the message: `expect(() => raise(A_upper, g_inv, 'μ')).toThrow(/already upper|variance/i)`.

findings.title: 'rejects raise() when label is absent from operand free indices' does not assert error type
findings.description: Same problem as the 'already upper' test: bare `.toThrow()` cannot distinguish a deliberate `LabelNotFoundError` from an accidental `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. The TENSOR-RULE `raise-requires-label-present-in-operand` is a named invariant and deserves a named assertion.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert the specific error class or message: `expect(() => raise(A_lower, g_inv, 'ν')).toThrow(LabelNotFoundError)` (or equivalent). If the library does not yet export a dedicated class for this, that is itself a forward-compat gap worth filing separately.

findings.title: Fresh-label collision test comment is internally inconsistent and the assertion is weaker than claimed
findings.description: The comment says 'raise(..., "μ") must NOT pick "α" as the fresh label' and then asserts `renamed[0] !== 'α'`. However, `g_inv` has two upper indices labelled `α` and `β`. When `raise` contracts the `μ` index of `A` against one of `g_inv`'s indices (say `α`), the *other* index of `g_inv` (`β`) becomes the free output index. The alpha-conversion is only needed if that surviving index collides with an existing free index of `A`. The test correctly checks that the fresh label is not `α`, but it does NOT check that the fresh label is not `μ` (which is being contracted and therefore disappears — but a buggy implementation could reuse it). More critically, the test does not assert `result.freeIndices.has('μ')` is `false`, so a broken implementation that fails to contract `μ` would still pass the `freeIndices.size === 2` check if it happened to produce two entries for other reasons.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `expect(result.freeIndices.has('μ')).toBe(false);` to confirm the contracted index is gone. Also assert the fresh label is not `'μ'`: `expect(renamed[0]).not.toBe('μ')`. Optionally assert `renamed[0] === 'β'` if the spec mandates a specific fallback sequence (ties into TENSOR-RULE `raise-lower-fresh-label-deterministic`).

findings.title: No test validates that raise/lower preserves the operand's physical dimensions
findings.description: Every test checks structural properties (kind, freeIndices, ok) but none asserts that the resulting tensor-product node carries the correct physical dimensions. The metric is DIMENSIONLESS, so `raise(A_μ [POTENTIAL], g_inv [DIMENSIONLESS], 'μ')` should yield a result with dimensions equal to POTENTIAL. If the implementation accidentally multiplies dimensions instead of inheriting them, all existing tests still pass. This is especially important as a forward-compat guard for v0.3.5 (mathjs numerical backend) where dimensional correctness will be evaluated numerically.
findings.suggested_fix: After `const result = validate(raised);`, add: `expect(result.dimensions).toEqual(POTENTIAL);` (or whatever the validator's dimension-output field is named). Add a second test with a dimensionful metric to confirm dimension multiplication is handled correctly.

findings.title: No round-trip test: raise then lower (or vice versa) should yield the original free-index structure
findings.description: The TENSOR-RULE `raise-lower-construct-tensor-product` implies that raise and lower are inverses (up to contraction). There is no test that performs `lower(raise(A_μ, g_inv, 'μ'), g, <freshLabel>)` and checks that the result contracts back to a scalar or recovers the original index structure. This is a critical forward-compat gap for v0.4.0 (Christoffel symbols require exactly this pattern).
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test: `const raised = raise(A_lower, g_inv, 'μ'); const freshLabel = [...validate(raised).freeIndices.keys()].find(l => l !== 'μ'); const roundTripped = lower(raised, g, freshLabel!); const rt = validate(roundTripped); expect(rt.ok).toBe(true); expect(rt.freeIndices.size).toBe(0);` — or whatever the expected contracted structure is.

findings.title: Determinism test only checks JSON equality of AST nodes, not the specific fresh label value
findings.description: The test `JSON.stringify(r1) === JSON.stringify(r2)` confirms that two calls with identical inputs produce identical AST output, which is good. However, it does not verify *what* the deterministic label is. TENSOR-RULE `raise-lower-fresh-label-deterministic` presumably specifies a concrete algorithm (e.g., 'pick the first label in a canonical Greek-letter sequence not in the collision set'). Without asserting the actual label value, a future refactor could change the label-generation algorithm and break downstream serialized expressions without this test catching it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `const freshLabel = [...validate(r1).freeIndices.keys()][0]; expect(freshLabel).toBe('β');` (substituting the actual expected label per the spec). This pins the deterministic output to a concrete value.

findings.title: No test for lower() with a multi-index operand
findings.description: The multi-index test at line 120 only covers `raise`. There is no symmetric test for `lower(T^{μν}, g, 'μ')` leaving `ν:upper` intact. Given that `lower` has its own alpha-conversion path, a bug specific to `lower`'s fresh-label logic on multi-index tensors would go undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a mirror test: `const T = tsym('T', [{label:'μ',variance:'upper'},{label:'ν',variance:'upper'}], POTENTIAL); const lowered = lower(T, g, 'μ'); const result = validate(lowered); expect(result.ok).toBe(true); expect(result.freeIndices.get('ν')).toEqual({upper:1,lower:0}); /* one new lower free index */`

findings.title: Metric constructed with signature string '+,-,-,-' but signature is never validated in tests
findings.description: The `metric()` constructor accepts a signature string. No test checks that passing an invalid signature (e.g., `'++--'` with wrong length, or a non-standard character) throws `MetricSignatureError`. This matters for v0.4.0 (Christoffel symbols) where the signature determines the sign of Christoffel terms. If `MetricSignatureError` is not exercised for the signature parameter itself, a regression in signature parsing could silently produce wrong Christoffel symbols.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `it('metric() rejects malformed signature string', () => { expect(() => metric('bad', [{label:'α',variance:'upper'},{label:'β',variance:'upper'}], DIMENSIONLESS, '+-+')).toThrow(MetricSignatureError); });`

findings.title: freeIndices iteration pattern is repeated three times with no helper
findings.description: The pattern `let total = 0; for (const counts of result.freeIndices.values()) total += counts.upper;` appears three times. This is a test-internal style issue, but if `freeIndices` type changes in v0.3.5 (e.g., to a plain object), all three sites need updating. A local helper would reduce maintenance surface.
findings.suggested_fix: Add at top of describe block: `const sumUpper = (fi: Map<string,{upper:number,lower:number}>) => [...fi.values()].reduce((s,c) => s+c.upper, 0);` and similarly `sumLower`. Replace the three loops with `expect(sumUpper(result.freeIndices)).toBe(1);`

strengths: Explicitly references TENSOR-RULE identifiers in comments, creating a direct traceability link between spec invariants and test cases.
Tests both the structural output (kind, args.length) and the semantic output (freeIndices, ok) of validate(), not just that no exception is thrown.
Covers the asymmetric error cases (raise with lower metric, lower with upper metric) as distinct tests rather than collapsing them, making failure diagnosis easier.
The fresh-label collision test (line 86) is a non-trivial scenario that directly exercises the alpha-conversion invariant with a realistic index collision setup.
The determinism test (line 112) is a good regression guard for any future change to the label-generation algorithm.
The multi-index operand test (line 120) correctly checks that the untouched index retains its exact variance counts, not just that the size is 2.

summary: Three shallow smoke-tests that verify substring presence in error messages; they confirm the error classes exist and produce non-empty messages, but they do not exercise the TENSOR-RULE invariants they claim to cover, leave several important behaviours untested, and contain one latent false-positive risk.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE 'variance-mismatch-suggests-raise-lower' is only half-tested: the 'lower' variance path is never exercised
findings.description: Both VarianceMismatchError tests construct the error with variance='upper'. The TENSOR-RULE requires the message to suggest raise() when the index is lower and lower() when the index is upper (i.e. the suggestion should be the *opposite* operation). Passing 'upper' and checking that the message contains both 'raise(' and 'lower(' does not verify that the correct directional hint is given — an implementation that always emits both words regardless of variance would pass. The 'lower' variance path is never instantiated, so a regression that silently drops the hint for lower-variance mismatches would go undetected.

findings.title: No test verifies that VarianceMismatchError is an instance of Error (or a known base class), so catch-site behaviour is untested
findings.description: The raise/lower helpers introduced in v0.3.0 are expected to throw VarianceMismatchError at call sites that catch Error. If VarianceMismatchError does not extend Error (e.g. it is a plain object or extends a non-standard base), those catch blocks will silently swallow it or rethrow unexpectedly. No test checks instanceof Error, instanceof VarianceMismatchError, or that err.name is set correctly.

findings.title: No test verifies that VarianceMismatchError and IndexLabelCollisionError are actually thrown by the library functions that are supposed to throw them
findings.description: All three tests construct error objects directly via `new`. This means the tests would pass even if raise(), lower(), and the Einstein-contraction path never actually throw these error types — they could throw a generic Error or nothing at all. The TENSOR-RULE invariants ('variance-mismatch-suggests-raise-lower', 'index-collision-includes-helper-context') are only meaningful at the throw site, not at the constructor.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE 'index-collision-includes-helper-context' is under-specified: only 'Rename' is checked, not the alpha-conversion helper name
findings.description: The TENSOR-RULE comment says the collision error must include 'helper context'. v0.3.0 adds internal alpha-conversion; the natural helper context to surface is the name of the alpha-conversion function or a concrete rename example. Checking only for the word 'Rename' (a generic English word) does not verify that the message actually references the alpha-conversion API or provides an actionable example index name. A message like 'Rename your variable' would pass but give the user no actionable guidance.

findings.title: IndexLabelCollisionError second argument (arity/position '3') is never tested for semantic meaning — could be a count, an index position, or a depth
findings.description: The test passes the literal number 3 and checks that '3' appears somewhere in the message. It does not verify what '3' represents (collision count? tensor rank? index position?), so a future refactor that changes the argument semantics would still pass this test. This is a documentation gap that will cause confusion when v0.4.0 adds Christoffel symbols with rank-3 tensors.

findings.title: No negative / boundary tests: empty label string, null variance, or duplicate label with count=0 are not exercised
findings.description: Error constructors are often the first place undefined/null inputs surface at runtime. With v0.3.5 (mathjs backend) and v0.4.0 (Christoffel) consuming these errors, a constructor that crashes on an empty label or throws a second error inside the first error's constructor would be very hard to debug. No boundary inputs are tested.

findings.title: toContain('3') in IndexLabelCollisionError test is a false-positive risk: '3' could appear in boilerplate text unrelated to the argument
findings.description: expect(err.message).toContain('3') will pass if the message contains any digit '3' for any reason — e.g. 'v0.3.0', 'index 3', 'at position 3 in stack'. This is not a confirmed bug in the current message text, but it is a fragile assertion that could mask a regression where the actual collision count is dropped from the message.

findings.title: No test imports or references the new v0.3.0 AST node types (metric-tensor, kronecker-delta, tensor-partial-derivative), leaving their error paths completely uncovered
findings.description: The file is scoped to error discoverability but only covers two error classes. v0.3.0 adds three new AST node types; any errors they produce (e.g. misuse of a partial-derivative node with a wrong index variance) are not represented. When v0.4.0 adds covariant derivatives these error paths will be load-bearing.
findings.suggested_fix: Either extend this file or create a companion file that imports the new AST node constructors and verifies that invalid constructions throw typed, message-rich errors consistent with the TENSOR-RULE invariants.

strengths: The test file correctly imports from the typed errors module rather than catching generic Error objects, which means it will fail fast if the error classes are renamed or moved.

Separating label+variance presence (test 2) from the actionable-hint presence (test 1) is a good decomposition — a regression that drops the label from the message would be caught independently of one that drops the hint.
The TENSOR-RULE comments are co-located with the tests they are meant to enforce, making traceability to the spec straightforward.
Using vitest's toContain for substring checks is appropriate for human-readable error messages where exact wording may evolve.

summary: A two-entry placeholder test file that defers inverse-metric consistency checks to v0.3.5. The file is structurally sound as a deferral marker, but has several forward-compat and doc-clarity issues worth addressing before v0.3.5 work begins.

findings.title: No import of the types/symbols the todo tests will actually exercise, making v0.3.5 activation non-trivial to verify
findings.description: When a developer activates these todos in v0.3.5 they will need to import `MetricTensor`, `KroneckerDelta`, `ValidationResult`, and the contraction/raise-lower helpers. Because none of those symbols are imported (even as commented-out stubs), there is no compile-time signal if those APIs are renamed or removed between now and v0.3.5. A broken import would be caught immediately at activation time rather than silently drifting. This is especially risky given that v0.3.0 is explicitly described as a 'forward-compat prerequisite'.

findings.title: Second todo conflates a ValidationResult schema change with a behavioural test, risking scope confusion at v0.3.5
findings.description: The todo `"v0.3.5 — ValidationResult.violations gains severity:'error'|'warning' field"` describes a *type/schema change*, not a test assertion. When activated it will need to be split: one test for the new field's presence/type (a schema test) and one for the actual warning being emitted on g·g⁻¹ ≠ δ. Keeping them as a single todo risks a future implementer writing only a schema test and shipping without the behavioural assertion, or vice versa. The first todo already covers the behavioural side partially, so the boundary is ambiguous.

findings.title: File header references `v0.3.0-Design.md §13 Q2` but does not state what the Violation.severity field looks like, leaving the contract underspecified for the v0.3.5 implementer
findings.description: The comment says the `Violation.severity` field is a 'substantive enrichment' deferred to v0.3.5, but does not record the agreed shape (e.g. `severity: 'error' | 'warning'`). A developer picking this up in v0.3.5 must go back to the design doc to recover the contract. If the design doc evolves, the test file gives no hint that it is stale. The todo text on line 16 partially captures this, but only inside the test name string — not in a machine-checkable or easily grep-able form.
findings.suggested_fix:
Extend the file header comment:
```typescript
 * Deferred schema addition (v0.3.5):
 *   interface Violation { severity: 'error' | 'warning'; ... }
 * The contraction g_ij * g^jk should produce delta_i^k;
 * deviation triggers severity:'warning'.
```

findings.title: No todo for the identity-index variance case: g_ij · g^jk must yield a mixed-variance Kronecker delta, not a covariant or contravariant one
findings.description: The existing todo checks that the contracted result equals the Kronecker delta, but does not specify that the result must be the *mixed-variance* delta (one lower, one upper index). This is a distinct invariant from the numerical equality check and is exactly the kind of variance-typing that the v0.3.0 tensor algebra layer is designed to enforce. Without a todo for it, v0.3.5 may ship a numerically correct but variance-incorrect result that passes the existing todo.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add:
```typescript
it.todo("v0.3.5 — g_ij · g^jk contraction result carries mixed variance (one covariant, one contravariant index), not fully covariant/contravariant");
```

findings.title: The `describe` block label says 'deferred to v0.3.5' but the file header says the same; the redundancy is harmless but the describe label will appear verbatim in CI output forever until v0.3.5, which may confuse contributors
findings.description: Minor: the describe string `'Inverse-metric consistency (deferred to v0.3.5)'` will appear in every CI run's test report as a pending suite. This is intentional, but the parenthetical version tag will become stale noise after v0.3.5 ships. A `@version` annotation in the comment block is more durable than embedding the version in the runtime-visible describe string.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `describe('Inverse-metric consistency', () => {` and rely on the file-header comment for the deferral rationale. Alternatively keep the label but add a lint rule or TODO comment to strip the parenthetical at v0.3.5.

strengths: Explicit design-doc citation (v0.3.0-Design.md §13 Q2) gives a clear audit trail for the deferral decision — this is good practice for a multi-version library.
Using `it.todo` rather than `it.skip` or a commented-out block is the correct Vitest idiom: todos appear in the test report as pending, keeping the gap visible in CI without failing the suite.
The two todos cleanly separate the behavioural concern (contraction result) from the schema concern (Violation.severity), which is the right decomposition even if the boundary needs sharpening.
The file is intentionally minimal — it does not import unused symbols or write speculative implementation code, which keeps the v0.3.0 diff clean.

summary: The test suite covers basic JSON round-trip mechanics for the three new v0.3.0 AST node types, but several tests are weaker than their names imply: they conflate structural equality with true losslessness, miss prototype/class-instance fidelity, and leave critical validator integration almost untested. The pderiv test also constructs its inputs in a way that may not exercise the wrtIndex path it claims to.

findings.title: Round-trip tests use plain-object equality, not AST-node identity — class instances silently lose their prototype after JSON.parse
findings.description: All three round-trip tests call JSON.parse and then compare with toEqual, which only checks structural (deep-value) equality. If metric(), kronecker(), or pderiv() return class instances (or objects with non-enumerable properties, Symbol keys, or methods), JSON.parse produces a plain object that passes toEqual but is not a valid AST node for downstream consumers. The test name claims 'lossless' but does not verify that validate(parsed) actually reconstructs a typed node — it only checks that the plain object happens to have the same enumerable values. This is especially dangerous as a forward-compat prerequisite for v0.3.5 (mathjs backend) which will likely call methods on these nodes.

findings.title: validate() integration test only checks ok and inferredDimension — error messages and index-variance metadata are not compared
findings.description: The 'metric-tensor round-trips losslessly' test calls validate() on both the original and the parsed node and compares only ok and inferredDimension. If the validator also returns index variance information, error details, or a normalized AST, those fields are silently dropped from the assertion. A round-trip that corrupts index labels (e.g. Unicode normalization of 'μ') would still pass this test because inferredDimension for DIMENSIONLESS is trivially {}.
findings.suggested_fix:
Replace the two-field comparison with a full deep-equal on the entire validate result:
```typescript
expect(roundtripped).toEqual(original);
```
Also add a test where the metric has non-trivial dimension (e.g. LENGTH) so inferredDimension is non-empty and actually exercises the comparison.

findings.title: pderiv test constructs x with an 'upper' index but wrtIndex is 'lower' — the test does not verify that this variance mismatch is handled correctly
findings.description: x is constructed with { label: 'α', variance: 'upper' } while wrtIndex is { label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }. The test name claims to verify 'wrtIndex nested object' serialization, but it never asserts anything about the relationship between x's index variance and wrtIndex's variance. More importantly, it does not call validate(dPhi), so it is unknown whether this combination is semantically valid. If pderiv() is supposed to enforce that wrtIndex matches the coordinate index variance (or its dual), this test would pass even if that invariant is broken.
findings.suggested_fix: Add validate(dPhi) and assert the expected ok value. Also add a second case where wrtIndex.label matches x's index label to confirm the intended usage, and a negative case where variance is mismatched to confirm the validator rejects it.

findings.title: kronecker-delta round-trip test has no validate() call and no assertion on index variances
findings.description: The kronecker test only checks structural equality of the serialized node. It does not assert that the delta has one upper and one lower index (the standard Kronecker delta invariant), nor does it call validate(). A regression that swaps both indices to 'lower' would pass this test. This is particularly important for v0.4.0 (Christoffel symbols) which will contract Kronecker deltas.

findings.title: Idempotent-serialization test ('second pass') only tests metric, not kronecker or pderiv
findings.description: The 'round-tripped nodes serialize identically on second pass' test only exercises metric(). If pderiv() or kronecker() contain any non-deterministic key ordering (e.g. from object spread order or conditional property insertion), the second-pass idempotency would not be caught. This is a gap given that pderiv has a nested wrtIndex object which is the most likely source of key-order instability.

findings.title: No negative / invalid-input round-trip tests — validator path for malformed parsed nodes is untested
findings.description: All tests use well-formed inputs. There are no tests for what happens when JSON.parse produces a node with a missing required field (e.g. no 'signature' on a metric node, or no 'wrtIndex' on a pderiv node). The validator is called only once (in the metric test) and only on a valid node. For a library that is a forward-compat prerequisite, the validator's behavior on deserialized-but-corrupt nodes is important to pin down.
findings.suggested_fix: Add at least one test per node type where a required field is deleted from the parsed object before calling validate(), and assert that validate() returns ok: false with a meaningful error message.

findings.title: LENGTH dimension constant is defined locally but DIMENSIONLESS is imported — inconsistency risks drift
findings.description: DIMENSIONLESS is imported from types.js but LENGTH is defined inline as a literal. If the canonical LENGTH constant in types.js ever changes its shape (e.g. gains a new base dimension for v0.4.0), the inline definition will silently diverge and tests using LENGTH will no longer match the library's own type system.
findings.suggested_fix:
Import LENGTH from types.js alongside DIMENSIONLESS:
```typescript
import { DIMENSIONLESS, LENGTH } from '../../src/dimensional/types.js';
```
If LENGTH is not yet exported, export it and use it here.

findings.title: No test for round-tripping a metric node with a non-Minkowski signature — forward-compat gap for Christoffel/Riemannian use in v0.4.0
findings.description: Both metric() calls use the Minkowski signature '+,-,-,-'. v0.4.0 will need Riemannian metrics (all '+' signature) for Christoffel symbols. If the signature field has any special-casing for Minkowski in the serializer or validator, a Riemannian metric might fail to round-trip. There is no test to catch this regression early.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test case with signature '+,+,+,+' (Euclidean/Riemannian) and assert it round-trips and validates correctly.

strengths: Correctly imports from the three distinct v0.3.0 source modules (metric.js, tensor.js, types.js) rather than a single barrel export, keeping test dependencies explicit.
The pderiv test explicitly checks parsed.wrtIndex, parsed.of, and parsed.wrt as separate assertions, which would catch a regression where nested objects are flattened during serialization.
The idempotency test (second-pass serialization) is a good pattern that catches non-deterministic key ordering bugs that toEqual would miss.

Using DIMENSIONLESS as the dimension for the metric tensor is semantically correct (the metric is dimensionless in natural units) and avoids introducing spurious dimension-mismatch failures in the round-trip tests.

summary: A thin preview test that checks `pderiv(g, x, μ)` produces a well-formed rank-3 tensor; the single live test is structurally reasonable but contains a subtle semantic error in how the derivative index is counted, and the test's relationship to the actual `pderiv` API contract is under-specified in ways that will cause silent regressions when v0.4.0 lands.

findings.title: `pderiv` denominator variable `x_coord` has an upper index, but the resulting derivative index is asserted as lower — the index-variance derivation is untested
findings.description: `x_coord` is declared with `variance: 'upper'` (a contravariant coordinate). Differentiation ∂/∂x^α lowers the free index to a covariant one, so the explicit third argument `{ label: 'μ', variance: 'lower' }` is passed separately. The test never checks that `pderiv` actually derives the output index variance *from* the denominator symbol's variance (i.e., that passing an upper-index denominator automatically produces a lower free index). Instead it passes the desired variance explicitly, meaning the test would pass even if `pderiv` ignored the denominator's variance entirely and just trusted the third argument. This is a test-coverage gap that masks a potential bug in `pderiv`'s variance-inference logic.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a second assertion variant where the third argument is omitted (if the API supports inference) and the result is still `lower`, OR add a negative test where `{ label: 'μ', variance: 'upper' }` is passed explicitly and `validate` returns `ok: false` (or a specific error). At minimum, document that the third argument is authoritative and the denominator variance is ignored.

findings.title: `freeIndices.size` assertion of 3 does not guard against index-label collision between `x_coord`'s index `α` and the metric indices
findings.description: `x_coord` carries index label `α` (upper). After `pderiv`, the denominator index `α` should be consumed (it is the differentiation variable), leaving only `μ`, `ν`, `λ` as free. The test asserts `size === 3` and checks those three labels, which implicitly confirms `α` is not free — but there is no explicit assertion that `α` is absent from `freeIndices`. If `pderiv` has a bug where it leaks the denominator index into the free set, `size` would be 4 and the test would catch it, but only incidentally. A direct `expect(result.freeIndices.has('α')).toBe(false)` makes the intent unambiguous and will survive a future refactor that changes label names.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `expect(result.freeIndices.has('α')).toBe(false);` immediately after the `size` assertion.

findings.title: No test for dimensional analysis of `pderiv` output — `∂g/∂x` should carry `LENGTH^{-1}` but is never checked
findings.description: `g_lower` is `DIMENSIONLESS` and `x_coord` has dimension `LENGTH`. The partial derivative `∂g/∂x` must therefore have dimension `LENGTH^{-1}`. The test validates structural well-formedness (`result.ok`, free indices) but never asserts `result.dimensions` (or equivalent). This is a critical gap for a library whose primary value proposition is dimensional analysis; a regression in `pderiv`'s dimension arithmetic would go undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: `expect(result.dimensions).toEqual({ L: -1, M: 0, T: 0, I: 0, Theta: 0, N: 0, J: 0 });` (adjust field name to match the actual `ValidationResult` shape).

findings.title: No negative / ill-formed test: repeated free index label across `pderiv` arguments is never exercised
findings.description: The preview test only covers the happy path. For v0.4.0 Christoffel construction, `pderiv` will be called with tensors that share index labels (e.g., `∂_ρ g_μν` where `ρ` also appears in the outer expression). There is no test that `validate` correctly rejects or flags a `pderiv` node where the differentiation index label collides with a free index of the operand (e.g., `pderiv(g_lower_νλ, x, { label: 'ν', variance: 'lower' })` — `ν` is already free in `g`). Without this, the alpha-conversion logic advertised in the v0.3.0 release notes is untested.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test: construct `pderiv(metric('g', [{label:'ν',...},{label:'λ',...}], ...), x_coord, {label:'ν', variance:'lower'})` and assert either that `validate` returns an error about index collision, or that alpha-conversion renames the internal index and `freeIndices` still has size 3 with the correct labels.

findings.title: The two `it.todo` stubs for Christoffel and covariant derivative lack any skeleton assertions, making them non-actionable for v0.4.0 implementors
findings.description: Both `it.todo` entries name the target formula but provide no expected API shape, no expected `freeIndices` structure, and no expected dimension. When v0.4.0 work begins, the implementor has no machine-checkable contract to implement against. For a library that explicitly tracks TENSOR-RULE invariants, this is a forward-compat gap.

findings.title: TENSOR-RULE tag `pderiv-of-metric-composes` is referenced in a comment but not defined anywhere in the visible spec
findings.description: The comment `// TENSOR-RULE: pderiv-of-metric-composes` implies a named invariant in the spec document, but the rule name does not appear in the v0.3.0 spec excerpt provided. If the rule is undefined, reviewers cannot verify the test actually exercises the stated invariant, and the tag provides false assurance.
findings.suggested_fix: Either add `pderiv-of-metric-composes` to the spec with a precise statement (e.g., 'pderiv(T, x, idx) is well-formed iff T is well-formed and idx.label ∉ contracted indices of T'), or rename the comment to `// building-block: pderiv-of-metric` to avoid implying a formal rule exists.

strengths: Correctly separates the v0.3.0 building-block test from the v0.4.0 Christoffel/covariant-derivative work via `it.todo`, keeping the test suite green without hiding future obligations.
Uses realistic physics labels (ν, λ, μ, α) and a Minkowski signature string '+,-,-,-', which will catch label-handling bugs that toy single-index tests would miss.
Asserting each free index individually (`freeIndices.get('μ')`, etc.) rather than just checking `size` is good practice and will catch variance-flip bugs.
Importing from the correct v0.3.0 module paths (`metric.js`, `tensor.js`) and using named exports keeps the test aligned with the public API surface.

summary: The drift-guard test is structurally sound and mirrors the Part-VII guard correctly, but contains two concrete bugs: a shared-state regex reuse bug that will silently drop markers on the second call to extractSpecRules, and a logical gap where the orphan-anchor comment claims to satisfy rule (a) for two rules but the test's own regex will match those comment lines and count them as test references, creating a circular self-fulfillment that masks genuinely untested rules. There are also forward-compat and api-ergonomics concerns worth addressing before v0.3.5.

findings.title: Module-level regex SPEC_MARKER_RE is stateful; second extractSpecRules call silently drops markers
findings.description: SPEC_MARKER_RE is declared once at module scope with the /g flag. extractSpecRules resets lastIndex to 0 before use, which is correct for a single call, but the function is called twice in the describe block: once for SPEC_PART_VIII and once for SPEC_PART_VII (lines ~55-56). Because the regex object is shared, if any interleaving or re-entrant execution occurs (e.g., Vitest worker parallelism, or a future refactor that calls extractSpecRules inside a beforeAll), lastIndex may be non-zero on the second call. More critically, TEST_REF_RE at line 33 is also module-level with /g and is reset inside indexTestReferences, but indexTestReferences is called once per file in a loop — the reset at line 65 only fires before the first file, not before each file. For every file after the first, TEST_REF_RE.lastIndex is left wherever the previous exec loop ended (which is 0 after the while loop exhausts, so this is actually safe in the happy path, but fragile). The real critical case: if the spec text for Part-VIII happens to end mid-match and lastIndex is non-zero when extractSpecRules is called for Part-VII, markers at the start of Part-VII will be skipped. The fix is to use local regex instances inside each function.

findings.title: Orphan-anchor comments self-fulfill rule (a): the drift guard marks itself as a test reference for the anchored rules
findings.description: The JSDoc block at the top of this file contains the literal strings 'TENSOR-RULE: pderiv-of-metric-composes' and 'TENSOR-RULE: v030-additive-semver-minor-bump'. TEST_REF_RE matches any occurrence of that pattern in any .test.ts file, including comments. Therefore indexTestReferences will find these two IDs in this very file and add it to their refs map. The it.each test for Part-VIII rules will then pass for these two IDs because refs is defined and non-empty — but the 'test reference' is just a comment in the drift-guard file itself, not an actual test exercising the rule. This means a genuinely untested Part-VIII rule could be silently whitelisted by adding it to the orphan-anchor comment block, defeating the purpose of the guard. The v0.4.0 todo anchor for pderiv-of-metric-composes is especially risky: when Task 12's test file lands, there will be a real reference, but until then the guard is green for the wrong reason.

findings.title: indexTestReferences resets TEST_REF_RE.lastIndex only once before the file loop, not per file
findings.description: TEST_REF_RE.lastIndex = 0 is set at line 65, before the for-of loop over files. Inside the loop, the while loop runs exec until it returns null, which resets lastIndex to 0 automatically on exhaustion — so in the normal case this is safe. However, if any file's text causes exec to throw (e.g., a file that cannot be decoded as UTF-8 but passes the .test.ts filter), lastIndex will be left at a non-zero value for the next file, causing the first N characters of that file to be skipped. This is a latent bug that becomes real if binary or non-UTF-8 test fixtures are added. The fix (local regex per file, as in finding #1) eliminates this entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Move TEST_REF_RE.lastIndex = 0 inside the for-of loop, or better, use a local regex instance per file (see finding #1 suggested fix).

findings.title: Hard-coded baseline count of 19 will silently pass if Part-VIII gains rules but the test file is not updated
findings.description: The assertion `expect(partVIIIRules.length).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(19)` is a floor, not a snapshot. When v0.3.5 or v0.4.0 adds Christoffel-symbol rules to Part-VIII, the count will grow but the test will never fail — it only catches regressions that remove rules below 19. For a drift guard, a snapshot (toEqual(N)) or a separate 'no rules were removed since last run' mechanism would be more useful. At minimum, a comment should document what the 19 rules are so a reviewer can verify the baseline is meaningful.

findings.title: listTestFiles will recurse into node_modules or dist if TESTS_DIR is misconfigured or symlinked
findings.description: listTestFiles performs an unbounded recursive walk from TESTS_DIR. If TESTS_DIR resolves to a path that contains a node_modules symlink or a dist/ folder with compiled .test.ts files (possible in some monorepo setups), the walk will index those files too, producing spurious test references. This is the same latent issue present in the Part-VII guard, but it becomes more acute as the test suite grows toward v0.4.0.

findings.title: Rule (b) bidirectional check does not distinguish Part-VII-only references from Part-VIII references, masking cross-spec pollution
findings.description: The 'every TENSOR-RULE reference in tests matches a real marker' test accepts any ID present in either Part-VII or Part-VIII. This means a test file could reference a Part-VII rule ID inside a Part-VIII-specific test (e.g., a metric-tensor test that accidentally references a Part-VII index-variance rule), and the guard would pass. For a drift guard whose stated purpose is Part-VIII coverage, it would be useful to separately report references that resolve only to Part-VII (not Part-VIII) so reviewers can confirm the cross-reference is intentional.

findings.title: it.each receives single-element tuple arrays, making test output show '[id]' instead of 'id'
findings.description: `partVIIIRules.map((id) => [id])` wraps each ID in an array, so Vitest's it.each receives `[[id1], [id2], ...]`. The test title template uses `%s` which will render the array as `["metric-tensor-symmetric"]` rather than `metric-tensor-symmetric`. This is a cosmetic issue but makes CI output harder to read.

findings.title: JSDoc says 'Part-VII OR Part-VIII' for rule (b) but the orphan-anchor comment conflates anchoring with satisfying rule (a)
findings.description: The comment states that the orphan-marker registry 'anchors' rules so 'the drift guard sees it during the v0.3.0 window'. This implies the comment is intentionally acting as a test reference, but the design doc rule (a) says 'referenced by at least one *.test.ts file' — a comment in a test file is not the same as a test exercising the rule. The documentation should explicitly state that these are deferred/meta rules exempt from rule (a), not that they are satisfied by the comment anchor.
findings.suggested_fix:
Rewrite the JSDoc to be explicit:

```
 * Deferred-rule registry (rules exempt from rule (a) during v0.3.0):
 *   pderiv-of-metric-composes — deferred to v0.4.0 Task 12; see DEFERRED_RULES below.
 *   v030-additive-semver-minor-bump — meta/release rule; no runtime AST binding.
 * These IDs must NOT appear as TENSOR-RULE: <id> strings in this file to avoid
 * self-fulfilling the bidirectional check.
```

strengths: Bidirectional guard design (spec→tests and tests→spec) is the correct approach for preventing drift in both directions simultaneously.
In-process file enumeration with no shell-out is correct for Windows compatibility and avoids CI environment fragility.
Explicit lastIndex reset before the extractSpecRules loop shows awareness of stateful regex pitfalls, even if the fix is incomplete.
Separating Part-VII and Part-VIII rule sets while unioning them for the orphan check is the right data model for a multi-part spec.
The deferred-rule concept (orphan-anchor registry) is a good forward-compat pattern; it just needs to be implemented without self-fulfillment.

summary: A focused structural test for the v0.3.0 eikonal null-geodesic form of BE-37. The suite is well-scoped and the helper is correct, but several gaps undermine the 'structural' claim: the index-variance contract is never checked, the RHS zero node is not inspected for kind correctness, the `hasKind` helper silently misses array-valued index fields, and there is no guard against the exported constants being `undefined` at import time.

findings.title: Index-variance contract (contravariant g^μν × covariant ∂_μ × covariant ∂_ν) is never asserted
findings.description: The test claims to verify the 'structural origin' of the eikonal equation, but it never checks that the metric-tensor node carries contravariant indices and that the two tensor-partial-derivative nodes carry covariant indices. A mis-typed AST (e.g. all covariant, or mixed incorrectly) would still pass every assertion here. For v0.4.0 Christoffel / covariant-derivative work, correct variance on these nodes is load-bearing; catching a variance bug now is far cheaper than debugging it in v0.4.0.

findings.title: `hasKind` silently skips array-valued `indices` / `slots` fields present on metric-tensor and tensor-partial-derivative nodes
findings.description: The helper recurses into `args`, `of`, and `wrt`, but v0.3.0 AST nodes for `metric-tensor` and `tensor-partial-derivative` may carry child nodes inside an `indices` array or a `slots` array (depending on the schema in Part-VIII). If the target kind ever appears nested inside such a field, `hasKind` returns `false` and the 'proves v0.3.0 surface' test silently passes for the wrong reason — or silently fails when the structure is correct. Because the test is the primary guard for the v0.3.0 surface claim, a silent miss is a critical reliability gap.

findings.title: RHS zero node is never inspected for structural kind — a plain `number` literal would pass
findings.description: The test asserts `rhs.freeIndices.size === 0` and `rhs.ok === true`, but never checks that `BE37_EIKONAL_RHS_ZERO` is an AST node of kind `'scalar'` (or `'literal'`, per the schema). If the export is a raw JavaScript `0` or any non-AST value that `validate` happens to accept, the structural claim is hollow. This matters because `validateEquation` comparing a rich LHS against a bare `0` could mask type-coercion bugs in the validator.

findings.title: No guard against `BE37_EIKONAL_LHS` / `BE37_EIKONAL_RHS_ZERO` being `undefined` at import time
findings.description: If the source module exports these constants conditionally or a future refactor renames them, every test in this file will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` rather than a clear assertion failure. Vitest will report the entire suite as errored rather than failed, making CI output harder to triage. This is especially risky because the exports are new in v0.3.0 and their names are not yet stabilised.

findings.title: Einstein contraction is asserted only indirectly via `freeIndices.size === 0`; the repeated dummy index pair (μ, ν) is never verified
findings.description: The test confirms the result is a scalar but does not verify that the scalar arises from a valid Einstein summation (one upper μ on g^μν contracted with one lower μ on ∂_μ S, and likewise for ν). A validator that simply strips all indices without checking the upper/lower pairing rule would still produce `freeIndices.size === 0`. For v0.4.0 Christoffel work, the contraction-pairing invariant is foundational.
findings.suggested_fix:
Expose a `contractedIndexPairs` or `summationPairs` field from `validate()` and assert:
```typescript
expect(lhs.contractedIndexPairs).toContainEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({ name: 'mu', upper: 'metric-tensor', lower: 'tensor-partial-derivative' })
);
```
If the validator does not yet expose this, file it as a forward-compat gap for v0.3.5 and add a TODO comment here.

findings.title: Dimensional homogeneity test does not verify the *units* of the intermediate factors, only the final scalar
findings.description: `validateBE37EikonalDimensions` returns `lhsDim === DIMENSIONLESS`, but this is consistent with both a correct encoding (g^μν is [L^-2] × ∂_μS is [L] × ∂_νS is [L] → dimensionless) and an incorrect one where all factors are declared dimensionless from the start. The test cannot distinguish these cases. A future numerical backend (v0.3.5) will rely on the per-factor dimensions being correct.

findings.title: `hasKind` is a useful utility that belongs in a shared test-helper module, not inlined per test file
findings.description: The same recursive AST-walking pattern will be needed by every structural test added for v0.3.0 bridges (BE-38, BE-39, etc.) and for v0.4.0 Christoffel tests. Duplicating it per file risks divergence (as already seen with the missing `indices`/`slots` field bug above).

findings.title: Test description for the third `it` conflates two distinct assertions in one sentence
findings.description: The string `'both sides have no free indices (eikonal LHS is a scalar contraction; RHS is the literal zero)'` bundles two separate structural claims. When one fails, the test runner output is ambiguous about which side is broken. This will become a triage burden as the suite grows.

strengths: The test file is correctly scoped to v0.3.0 structural concerns and explicitly defers numerical evaluation to the companion be-37-shapiro-encoding.test.ts — good separation of concerns.
`hasKind` correctly handles the non-standard `of`/`wrt` fields on `tensor-partial-derivative` nodes, showing awareness of the v0.3.0 AST schema.

Using `validateEquation` rather than two separate `validate` calls for the first test correctly exercises the equation-level validator, which is the right API surface for dimensional homogeneity of an equation.
The four-test structure maps cleanly onto four distinct invariants (equation validity, dimensional homogeneity, scalar rank, AST kind presence), making failures easy to localise.
The JSDoc header is thorough: it cites the planning doc, the spec section, the task number, and the companion test file — exactly the cross-referencing needed for a multi-version library.
